Overview

The question, what is known, and what is still open

A protein language model can guess what an enzyme does from its sequence alone. Point one at organisms it has never seen and it gets worse. This document measures how much worse, and how many proteins a scientist would have to label by hand to repair it.

The question

Someone sequences an unfamiliar organism — or scoops DNA straight out of seawater — and wants to know what its enzymes do. A model trained on well-studied bacteria will get some of them wrong. The fix is to label some proteins by hand, which is slow and expensive. How many have to be labelled? Call that fraction r*, the recovery threshold. How one measurement is made, end to end, is set out before the statistic that rests on it.

Real biology cannot answer this cleanly, because you cannot dial "how different are these organisms" smoothly and you never know the true answer. So a synthetic protein universe was built where distance is a dial, calibrated against measurements from real proteins, and swept. Three generations of that simulator, and the real-data runs that eventually checked it, are what this document records.

What the data says, as of 13 August 2026

Measured on 231,285 real Swiss-Prot proteins across 15 taxonomic groups with real enzyme labels, the quantity that behaves well turned out not to be r* at all. It is retention: the share of achievable performance that survives transfer before anything is labelled by hand.

Retention splits the 14 target groups into two blocks with nothing in the gap between them. Eight bacterial targets retain 0.71 to 1.00; six archaeal and eukaryotic targets retain 0.22 to 0.54. The boundary falls between 36.7% and 42.0% median sequence identity to the training set — straddling the ~40% threshold the enzyme-annotation literature already uses. That threshold was not fitted here, and its appearance was not planned.

The practical version. Above roughly 42% sequence identity to something already known, essentially no hand-labelling is needed. Below roughly 37%, between a third and a half of the labelling budget has to come from the new organisms. That is a prediction a scientist can make before labelling anything, from sequence alone.

r* itself proved fragile. It reads 0.0 for twelve of the fourteen targets at a budget of 200 proteins, reproduces the split at 1,000, and drifts at 2,000. It should never be quoted without the budget it was measured at. real dataEC labels · level 3job 47292627

What is not settled

Stated plainly, because these are the load-bearing weaknesses and they are easier to find here than buried on page nine.

StatusIssue
unresolved The simulator labels by family, not by function. Every synthetic number in this document is a homology recovery threshold being used to reason about a function problem. Building an enzyme-like label space hit a purity-versus-coverage conflict that is still not solved. This is the single most likely thing to be challenged, and it is answered here.
retracted β is not a damage knob. It was reported as one, then measured with the wrong sign on real data (ρ = +0.28), and the causal claim was withdrawn. Under a matched control it is mildly protective. The full history.
open The simulator predicts about three times more transfer damage than reality shows, and is 12× off on how much a shift rearranges class positions. It matches on geometry and fails on consequences; that gap is unexplained.
open Retention may be measuring database coverage rather than biology. It correlates with Pfam coverage at ρ = +0.86 (n = 14), and every sequence-identity claim here rests on 14 points from a single source group.
holds Function transfers better than homology in all four directions tested, so the functional readout is the more robust one, not the more fragile one.

Which cells have actually been measured

The thesis’s goal is to predict EC number (function). Until 7 August every recovery threshold ever measured here was a Pfam (homology) threshold. This is the table from BRIEF_ec_recovery_threshold.md, with the bottom-right cell now filled:

Family / Pfam labels homology EC labels function
Synthetic ✓r*(d), v1 and v2 sweeps. Jobs 46964648, 47136848. The label is the family the point was drawn from: a Pfam-like concept. ✗Never measured. The oracle was the attempt to manufacture an EC-like label space on top of family structure; it hit an unresolved purity/coverage conflict (§13) and the generator still labels by family. This cell is still empty.
Real ✓r* = 0.10–0.25. Swiss-Prot→TrEMBL (jobs 46973939/40) and the 5-domain taxonomy ladder (46980033–36). ✓Filled 7 Aug 2026. 14-target ladder, four arms, four budgets, three seeds: job 47292627. And the headline turned out not to be r* at all, but retention.
Note the top-right cell before quoting any synthetic number about function. Every synthetic r* on this page (§4, §10, §15) is a homology recovery threshold being used to reason about a function problem. That substitution is defensible (§20 Q4 shows both axes are structured in the same way, excess +0.52 to +0.64) but it is a substitution, and it is the single most likely thing to be challenged.

The three generator versions

Three generations. Each fixed a defect that made the previous one incapable of answering the question.

VersionHow labels workedHow the shift workedFatal flaw
v0
generate_simulation.py		 One frozen random network: the oracle: labelled both source and target Only tightened the source's variance around the same centroids Could never dip. Source was a nested subset of the target under the same labeller, so adaptation could only ever add information
v1
generate_synthetic_precomputed.py		 Oracle removed. Label = family index Each family displaced toward another family's position U-shaped ceiling. Difficulty moved with distance

B · Classifiers and macro-F1

Every headline number in this project is a macro-F1 score. If that phrase is fuzzy, nothing downstream can land. Here it is from scratch.

The model draws boundaries

Each protein is a dot in space. Each dot has a true label. The classifier's job is to carve space into regions and say "any dot landing here, I'll call class A". The dividing surfaces are the decision boundaries.

Training = adjusting those boundaries until they mostly put the right dots in the right regions.

Draw a boundary, then move the data underneath it

Two classes and the boundary a model learned. Now slide the data: the boundary stays where training left it. That is the entire mechanism of this thesis in one picture.

F1in-browser illustrationno dataDraw a boundary, then move the data underneath it
What it isA teaching illustration. Two classes of 2-D points, a boundary you place by hand, and a slider that slides the data under it.
DatasetNone. Points are generated in your browser from a fixed seed; no protein, real or synthetic, is involved.
What it stands in forThe mechanism behind negative transfer: a boundary that was correct becomes wrong when the data moves. §4 measures that for real.
ProvenanceDrawn live by this page. Not an experiment; nothing here is a measured number.
RelatedNothing; this is an illustration, not a run. See the catalogue for the experiments themselves.
Flip the mode button. "Everything slides" is covariate shift: both blobs move together, and although accuracy drops, the classes are still arranged the same way relative to each other. "Classes swap places" is concept shift: the boundary is now actively backwards. That distinction is exactly what α controls in the generator (§8).

What macro-F1 measures

The obvious score is accuracy; what fraction did you get right. It has a bad failure mode here: if 90% of your proteins are class A, a model that always says "A" scores 90% while being completely useless.

F1 for a single class balances two things:

precision = of the ones I called class A, how many really were? recall = of the ones that really are class A, how many did I catch? F1 = the harmonic mean of the two ← punishes you for being bad at either

Macro-F1 computes F1 separately for every class and then takes a plain average, so a tiny class counts exactly as much as a huge one. That's deliberate: our family sizes differ by 36×, and we don't want the score dominated by whichever enzyme happens to be well studied.

Rough feel for the numbers you'll see. Over ~90 classes, random guessing is about 0.01. Our shuffled-label control floors sit at 0.19–0.29 (not 0, because some classes are big enough to guess). A good model reaches 0.90–0.95. So when §16 says vertebrata retention is 0.22, that means zero-shot scored 0.21 where 0.95 was achievable: most of the way back down toward the floor.

C · Distance, spread and direction

Three geometric ideas the rest of the page leans on constantly. If §6 and §7 felt like word salad, it's because these weren't laid down first.

1 · Distance is just Pythagoras, repeated

2-D: ‖v‖ = √(x² + y²) 960-D: ‖v‖ = √(x₁² + x₂² + … + x₉₆₀²) same formula, more terms

Nothing exotic. "How far apart are two proteins" = this, applied to the difference of their two lists of 960 numbers.

2 · Spread (σ) is distance too

σ is the typical distance from a point to the middle of its own cloud. So you can compare it directly against the distance between clouds. That ratio is the whole ballgame:

gap ÷ σ ≫ 1 clouds far apart relative to their size → easy to tell apart gap ÷ σ ≈ 1 clouds overlap heavily → should be hard…

Real protein embeddings sit at gap ÷ σ ≈ 1.0 and yet classify at 0.90. That "impossible" combination is what §7 exists to explain, and it's the central design insight of the whole generator.

3 · Direction matters separately from distance

Two proteins can be equally far from you in completely different directions. Once you accept that "which way" is separate from "how far", three of the generator's knobs become obvious:

  • d = how far the target moved.
  • α = did all the classes move the same way, or each its own way?
  • β = did the move go along directions that matter for telling classes apart, or along directions the classifier ignores?

That's it. That's the whole shift model, before any maths.

SVD in full: a worked example, the interactive, and the link to PCA667 words

4 · SVD: how you find which directions matter

Ignore the name. "Singular Value Decomposition" tells you nothing. What it does:

SVD finds the natural axes of a cloud of points, ordered from longest to shortest. That's it. That is the whole idea.

Picture a rugby ball floating in space at some awkward angle. You want to describe its shape without knowing in advance how it's oriented. So you ask:

  1. Which single direction is this thing longest along? → that's axis 1, and its length is the first singular value.
  2. Now, among directions perpendicular to that one, which is longest? → axis 2.
  3. Repeat until you run out of dimensions.

You end up with a ranked list: direction, how much spread along it; direction, how much spread along it; …: sorted biggest first. "Singular value" is just the jargon for **how much spread**. Nothing more.

A worked example you can check

Take 400 points deliberately built as an ellipse with a long radius of 3.0, a short radius of 0.7, tilted 30°. Hand SVD only the raw point coordinates: no hint about the tilt or the radii. It returns:

direction 1: pointing 30.1° spread along it = 3.008 direction 2: pointing 120.1° spread along it = 0.697 share of total spread: direction 1 alone = 94.9%

It recovered the tilt and both radii from the points alone. That's all SVD ever does; it just does it in 960 dimensions instead of 2, where you can't eyeball it.

Reshape the cloud, watch SVD find its axes

The blue arrow is the direction SVD ranks first; the orange arrow is second. Change the tilt or squash the cloud and watch them follow.

F2in-browser illustrationno dataReshape the cloud, watch SVD find its axes
What it isLive SVD of a 2-D point cloud you reshape with sliders.
DatasetNone: browser-generated points.
What it stands in forThe same computation that defines B (the function subspace) on real embeddings in §20 Q2, and that sets the nuisance spectrum in the generator.
ProvenanceComputed live in the page. Not an experiment.
RelatedNothing; this is an illustration, not a run. See the catalogue for the experiments themselves.

Try making both radii equal. The cloud becomes a circle, both singular values match, and the "first" direction becomes arbitrary: there's no longest axis any more. That's what it looks like when a dataset has no preferred directions, and it's the opposite of what real embeddings do.

How we actually use it

input: 167 EC centroids × 960 numbers each (one row per EC class, in the source domain) SVD → 960 ranked directions, each with how much the centroids spread along it keep: the top 22, which together hold 90% of the spread → that is B, the "function subspace"

So B isn't chosen or designed: it's read off the data. "The directions along which EC classes differ from one another" is exactly "the directions the centroids spread along most", and SVD is the procedure that finds them.

And this is precisely where β goes wrong (§10, §20 Q2). SVD returns the directions ordered by spread. So B is, by construction, the widest directions, on our data the first is 11.3× wider than the 22nd. β then measures "how much of the move was inside B", which quietly means "how much of the move was along a roomy axis". The ordering is the whole bug.
If you've heard of PCA, it's the same thing. Principal Component Analysis on mean-centred data is SVD. Different name, same computation, same output. If someone says "the first principal component" they mean "SVD direction 1".
One notation habit worth absorbing: everything is quoted in multiples of the mean gap rather than raw units. "The shift is 1.2 gaps" means the classes moved 1.2× the typical distance between two class centres. It makes numbers comparable across datasets that have different scales.

D · How a model learns

You can't judge the r* argument without this. Everything below is the real mechanism, not an analogy, and the last demo trains a genuine neural network in your browser and reproduces the dip.

1 · A model is a pile of numbers. That's the whole thing.

Our classifier is four stacked multiplication tables. Nothing else is in there.

F3analytic / derivedno datathe MLP · 960→512→256→KThe classifier, layer by layer
What it isA diagram of the actual network used everywhere in this project, not a generic one.
Architecture960 → 512 → BatchNorm → ReLU → Dropout → 256 → ReLU → Dropout → K classes. 628,496 weights at K = 16.
Where it comes fromsrc/model.py; trained by src/train.py, adapted by src/adapt_OGadam.py.
ProvenanceStatic diagram. No data.
Relatedthe model itself
LayerTurnsIntoNumbers it holds
layer 1960 (the embedding)512492,032
batchnormrescales those 512 so they don't drift1,024
layer 2512256131,328
layer 3256one score per class4,112
total, for a 16-class problem628,496

Those 628,496 numbers: called weights: start off random. The model is garbage. "Training" is the process of nudging them until it isn't.

2 · One protein, forwards

960 numbers in → multiply by layer 1's table → 512 numbers → set anything negative to zero ("ReLU": the only non-linear step) → multiply by layer 2's table → 256 numbers → set negatives to zero again → multiply by layer 3's table → one score per class → highest score wins

That's a forward pass. Cheap, deterministic, no learning yet.

3 · Score the mistake

Compare those scores against the true answer. The loss is a single number summarising how wrong the model was, and crucially it punishes confident wrongness far more than hesitant wrongness.

How loss responds to confidence

Drag the model's confidence in the correct class. Note how the penalty explodes as confidence in the right answer approaches zero; that asymmetry is what stops models from bluffing.

F4analytic / derivedno datacross-entropy lossHow loss responds to confidence
What it isThe cross-entropy curve −log(p), plotted exactly.
DatasetNone. It is a function, not a measurement.
Where it comes fromThe same loss src/train.py minimises.
ProvenanceAnalytic. Nothing measured.
Relatedthe model itself

4 · Nudge every number downhill

For each of the 628,496 weights the computer asks: if I made this one slightly larger, would the loss go up or down, and how fast? The answer is a slope (a gradient), and getting all 628,496 of them at once is what backpropagation does.

Then every weight takes a small step downhill. How big a step is the learning rate: 0.001 in our case. This is the single most important knob in all of machine learning, and the demo below is the fastest way to understand why.

Gradient descent: roll the ball into the valley

The curve is the loss. The ball is your weights. Each step moves downhill by (slope × learning rate). Try a tiny rate, then crank it past 0.9 and watch it fly apart.

F5in-browser illustrationno dataGradient descent: roll the ball into the valley
What it isA 1-D toy loss surface with a real gradient-descent update applied per click.
DatasetNone.
What it stands in forThe optimiser inner loop. The real runs use Adam, not plain SGD: see the note under §F.
ProvenanceComputed live. Not an experiment.
RelatedNothing; this is an illustration, not a run. See the catalogue for the experiments themselves.
Three regimes, and all three matter to this project. Too small; it crawls; you run out of steps before arriving (that was estimator bug #2: one pass over the pool wasn't enough). Just right: smooth descent. Too big: it overshoots the valley and bounces out, ending up worse than it started. That is exactly the shape of negative transfer.

5 · Batches and epochs

You don't nudge after every single protein: too jumpy. You take a batch (32 or 256), average their slopes, and nudge once. A full sweep through all your data is an epoch.

source model: 4,000 proteins ÷ 256 per batch × 20 epochs = 320 nudges adaptation: 1,000 proteins ÷ 32 per batch × 1 pass = 32 nudges ← the bug

320 nudges to build the model; 32 to adapt it. That imbalance is why "one pass over the pool" was measuring the step count rather than what the pool contained.

6 · Watch a real network learn

A genuine neural network, training live

Two classes, a small network (2 → 8 → 2), trained by exactly the process above. The shaded regions are what it currently believes; the line is its decision boundary. Watch it go from random to correct.

F6in-browser illustrationno dataA genuine neural network, training live
What it isA real 2→8→2 MLP with real forward pass, real cross-entropy and real backprop, written out in the page’s JavaScript.
DatasetBrowser-generated 2-D points. No proteins.
Relation to the real modelSame maths, three orders of magnitude smaller (8 hidden units vs 512→256, 2 inputs vs 960).
ProvenanceTrains in your browser each time you press run. Not an experiment.
RelatedNothing; this is an illustration, not a run. See the catalogue for the experiments themselves.

Press reset a few times. Different random starting weights, same destination: the model finds a good boundary, not the good boundary. That non-uniqueness is why every result in this project is averaged over 3 seeds.

7 · Warm start, and the actual experiment

Now the part that the experiments here actually turn on. Adaptation does not start from random. It copies the source model's weights (already good at source proteins), and keeps nudging from there. That's a warm start.

The pool is 1,000 proteins. A fraction r of them come from the shifted target; the rest are more source proteins. The total never changes, only the mix.

One subtlety worth stating explicitly. r = 0 is not "do nothing". It's still 1,000 proteins and still 32 nudges: they're just all from the source. The model gets shaken up without being told anything new. That's the control that separates "did the composition matter" from "did any extra training matter", and it's why the dip can appear even at r = 0.

The whole experiment, in miniature: six classes, live

Six classes with deliberately unequal sizes (60, 45, 30, 20, 14, 10, like real protein families), scored with macro-F1, adapted in mini-batches. Step 1 trains a source model; step 2 rotates the world by d; step 3 adapts on a pool that is fraction r target.

F7in-browser illustrationno dataThe whole experiment, in miniature: six classes, live
What it isA miniature of the actual protocol: train on source, shift the world, then adapt on a pool whose composition r you control.
DatasetSix 2-D Gaussian classes generated in your browser. Not the synthetic generator and not real proteins.
Protocol it mirrorssource model → warm start → adapt on a fixed-size pool that is fraction r target → score on held-out target. Identical in shape to every r* run in this project.
ProvenanceRuns live in the page. Illustrative only; no number here should be quoted.
RelatedNothing; this is an illustration, not a run. See the catalogue for the experiments themselves.
What to try, in order. (1) d = 0: no shift. Everything lands near 0.90 whatever r is; adaptation neither helps nor hurts. (2) d = 0.20, r = 0: mild shift, no target data. It ends around 0.43, well below the 0.92 it could reach. (3) slide r up at d = 0.20: 0.43 → 0.46 → 0.54 → 0.61 → 0.65 → 0.92. That rising curve is the thesis. (4) d = 0.45, r = 0; the model is wrecked: macro-F1 ≈ 0.00. It needs r ≈ 0.35 before it climbs off the floor at all.
The dip is hard to produce, and that difficulty is itself a finding. Press "show me a dip" and you'll get one (about 8 points). But hunt around and you'll notice dips only appear at small d, where zero-shot is still decent; you can only fall if you're standing somewhere. At large d the model is already at the floor and can only go up.

This is exactly the history in §12: the original generator could never produce a dip at all, for structural reasons, and diagnosing that is what started the whole rebuild. If this toy makes the dip look fragile, that's not a flaw in the toy.
And notice the toy reproduces one of the August estimator bugs, for free. Whatever you set, r* comes out at or near 1.0, because the bar is "90% of a model trained properly on the whole target world", while adaptation gets only 90 mini-batches over 120 pooled points. The bar is out of reach for the budget, so r* stops measuring the shift and starts measuring the budget. That is estimator defect (d) in §16, live in front of you.

E · Inside ESM-C

§2 said "a model reads the protein and outputs 960 numbers" and left it there. What is actually happening, because "what does the embedding mean?" is a question you should be able to answer.

The trick: it was never trained to do our job

ESM-C is a protein language model. It was trained on millions of protein sequences with one absurdly simple task:

M K T A ? Y L V G … hide one amino acid guess what belongs in the ?

That's it. No labels, no EC numbers, no structures. Just: cover up a residue and predict it from its neighbours. Do that across a large fraction of all known protein sequences and something useful falls out, because to guess the missing residue well you have to implicitly learn what makes a protein a working protein: which residues pair up, which regions fold together, which patterns belong to which families, which substitutions are tolerated.

This is why we get the embedding for free. Nobody annotated anything. The model was solving a fill-in-the-blank puzzle, and the internal representation it built in order to solve that puzzle turns out to encode structure, family and function. We just read that representation out and throw the puzzle-answer away.

How it reads a sequence: attention

The architecture is a transformer. The one idea you need from it is attention: when the model processes residue 40, it doesn't just look at residues 39 and 41: it looks at every residue in the protein at once, and learns how much to weight each one.

That matters biologically. Two residues 200 positions apart in the sequence can be touching in the folded protein. A model that only read neighbours would never see that; attention can.

From a sequence to one vector

sequence of L amino acids → ESM-C → one 960-number vector per residue shape (L, 960) → average them all together "mean pooling" → one 960-number vector for the whole protein

That averaging step is worth flagging: it is crude. A 200-residue protein and a 2,000-residue protein both collapse to 960 numbers, and any information about where in the sequence something happened is discarded. It's standard practice, it works well, and it is also a place where information is definitely being thrown away.

Practical details from our pipeline. We use ESM-C 300M (300 million parameters, 960-dim output). Sequences are capped at 1,022 residues. Embedding all 231,285 proteins took about 2 hours on one A100 GPU. The output is a single 231,285 × 960 matrix (768 MB), and every analysis in this project reads that one file rather than re-running the model.
The exposure you should know about. ESM-C is, on published benchmarks, the best taxonomic classifier of any protein language model tested: its embeddings identify which organism a protein came from more accurately than competitors. We are using it to study taxonomic transfer. So there is a real possibility that what we measure is partly the embedding's sensitivity to taxonomy rather than a fact about biology. Repeating one arm with ESM-2 would separate those, and it hasn't been done. This is listed in §18 and it is the single best "what would you do next" answer.

F · The classifier, layer by layer

Eight lines of code, and every one of them is doing something you can name. The definition is:

nn.Linear(960, 512)      # 1. mix
nn.BatchNorm1d(512)      # 2. re-centre and re-scale
nn.ReLU()                # 3. bend
nn.Dropout(0.1)          # 4. randomly silence 10%

nn.Linear(512, 256)      # 5. mix again
nn.ReLU()                # 6. bend again
nn.Dropout(0.1)          # 7. silence again

nn.Linear(256, K)        # 8. one score per EC class

1, 5, 8 · Linear: the only layers that hold knowledge

A Linear layer is a matrix multiply: every output is a weighted sum of every input. These are the layers containing the 628,496 learned numbers. Everything else in the list has almost no parameters: it's plumbing.

On its own, stacking linear layers is pointless: a matrix times a matrix is just another matrix, so three linear layers in a row can only ever do what one could. Which is why you need…

3, 6 · ReLU: the bend that makes depth worth anything

ReLU(x) = max(0, x) negatives → 0, positives unchanged

Almost insultingly simple, and it's the entire reason a deep network can do more than a shallow one. Because it's non-linear, stacking layers now builds genuinely new shapes rather than collapsing back to one matrix.

Intuition: each ReLU unit is a switch that turns on past some threshold. With 512 of them you can carve space into a huge number of regions and give each its own behaviour, which is how the model draws a boundary that isn't a straight line.

2 · BatchNorm, and it matters more here than anywhere else

After the first Linear, the 512 outputs might be wildly different scales: one hovering near 0.001, another near 500. That makes training miserable: one learning rate can't suit both.

BatchNorm fixes it by standardising each of the 512 outputs across the current batch: subtract the batch's mean, divide by its standard deviation, then apply two learned numbers (a scale and an offset) so the network can undo it if it wants.

Why this one layer deserves your attention. BatchNorm keeps running averages of the mean and spread it has seen. Those statistics are computed from your training data, so a model trained on gammaproteobacteria carries around a memory of "this is what normal looks like", calibrated to bacteria.

Point it at plant proteins and those statistics are simply wrong. This is a genuine, mechanical part of why performance drops on a new taxonomic group, and it's fixable without any labels at all, just by recomputing the statistics on the new data.

That isn't speculation: in the July study, batch-norm recalibration was the best-performing adaptation method on all five real shifts; beating optimal-transport alignment, which was the best method on synthetic data and the worst on real. This is the most directly actionable result in the project.

4, 7 · Dropout: deliberate sabotage

During training only, Dropout randomly sets 10% of the values to zero each step. It sounds destructive, and it is: deliberately. It stops the network leaning too hard on any single feature, because that feature might vanish next step. The result generalises better. At test time dropout is switched off and everything is used.

8 → the answer: softmax and cross-entropy

The last Linear gives K raw scores, one per EC class: arbitrary numbers, possibly negative. Two more steps turn that into a decision and a penalty:

softmax exponentiate every score, divide by the total → K numbers between 0 and 1 that sum to 1 probabilities cross-entropy loss = −log( probability given to the correct class ) this is the curve you dragged in §D3

And the thing that does the nudging: Adam

§D described taking a step downhill of size (slope × learning rate). Plain SGD does exactly that. We use Adam, which is smarter in two ways: it keeps a running average of recent slopes (momentum, so it doesn't zig-zag), and it gives each weight its own effective step size based on how volatile that weight's slope has been. Weights with consistent slopes take big steps; jumpy ones take small steps.

Practically: Adam is far more forgiving of a badly-chosen learning rate, which is why it's the default. Ours is 0.001.

Two asymmetries in this architecture that look like typos but are deliberate. (1) There is a BatchNorm after the first Linear but not after the second. (2) The hidden layer widths shrink (960 → 512 → 256 → K) funnelling toward a decision rather than expanding. Neither is unusual, but both were inherited rather than chosen, and neither has been ablated. The architecture was never tuned: it was fixed early and held constant so that everything else could be compared fairly.

The argument

The question

What r* is, why it is hard to measure, and why synthetic data was needed

What the project is trying to measure, stated before any machinery. The biology, what an embedding is, why 960 dimensions behaves strangely, the definition of the recovery threshold r* and the dip that makes it interesting, and finally why any of this needed fake data at all.

0 · Motivation

The scenario the whole thesis is built around, taken verbatim from the generator's own documentation:

"A scientist pulls a metagenome from the deep Arctic and feeds it to a PLM. Those proteins belong to families we already have names for, but they sit some distance away from the human-biased region of sequence space the PLM was trained on. The model is confidently wrong at first, gets worse as the scientist adds a few of the new proteins, and only past some threshold r* does it beat where it started. We want: how many novel proteins must they sequence, as a function of how far out they went?"

Three things in that paragraph are the entire thesis:

  • "confidently wrong at first": the model doesn't know it's out of its depth.
  • "gets worse as the scientist adds a few"; this is negative transfer, and it's counterintuitive enough that it's worth a whole section (§4). Adding correct new data makes performance drop before it climbs.
  • "as a function of how far out they went": the goal isn't one number, it's a curve. r* as a function of distance. That's what makes it predictive rather than descriptive.
Note before proceeding: three words in this project mean different things in different notes, and it is the single biggest source of confusion.

1. "v1" and "v2" are overloaded three ways.

Where you see itWhat it means there
june17_premeeting.md §5three runs of the real-data experiment (5 families → 16 families → 16 families × 3 seeds)
JULY22.md, figures/README.mdgenerators: v1 = the July 14 build, v2 = its July 22 replacement
the original pre-June generatornever called "v1": just "the old pipeline". Already dead by July 14

So there are two separate generator rewrites, and the famous moving-ceiling bug belongs to the second generator, not the original one. This page calls them v0 / v1 / v2 and never anything else.

2. r* was silently redefined in July.

  • June definition: the smallest r at which the dip appears: onset of negative transfer.
  • July onward: the smallest r that recovers to 90% of the ceiling.

Every number after mid-July uses the second one. It is also the definition that depends on a ceiling: the seed of nearly every subsequent error.

3. "domain" ≠ "subspace". A domain is a group of organisms. A subspace is a set of directions in embedding space. β is about the second one only.

1 · Proteins, EC numbers and Pfam families

You said EC numbers are fine, so briefly: an EC number like 2.7.1.11 is a four-level code for the reaction an enzyme catalyses. Level 1 is the broad class (2 = transferase), level 2 the subclass, level 3 the sub-subclass, level 4 the exact reaction. We work at level 3 (2.7.1) because level 4 is too fine; the field's own benchmarks show most level-4 errors are correct through level 3.

Pfam, and why it is not the same thing as function

Pfam is a catalogue of protein families, defined by shared ancestry rather than by function. Two proteins are in the same Pfam family if their sequences are similar enough that they almost certainly descend from a common ancestral protein.

Concretely, a Pfam family is built like this: someone takes a handful of clearly-related sequences, aligns them, and builds a statistical profile (a hidden Markov model) of what that family "looks like" position by position. Any new sequence scoring highly against that profile joins the family. Pfam has roughly 20,000 such families; our dataset touches 3,282 of them.

The distinction that matters for this whole project: Pfam = who you're related to (ancestry, homology). EC = what you do (chemistry, function). They are different labels on the same proteins, and they mostly (but not perfectly) agree.

Why "mostly but not perfectly" is the crux: relatives usually do similar chemistry, so Pfam predicts EC well. In our data, 86.8% of Pfam families map to exactly one EC class. That's convenient biologically and deeply inconvenient scientifically, because it means a model that looks like it's predicting function might just be recognising families. This is the "homology confound" and it comes back in §16.

One more term: taxonomic group. That's the branch of the tree of life an organism sits on: gammaproteobacteria, vertebrates, plants. In this project it's the axis we move along: train on one group, test on another. Pfam and EC are labels on proteins; taxonomic group is where the protein came from.

LabelAnswersExampleRole here
Pfam familyWho is it related to?PF00005 (ABC transporter)The label the synthetic generator uses
EC numberWhat reaction does it do?2.7.1The label the thesis actually cares about
Taxonomic groupWhat organism is it from?gammaproteobacteriaThe axis we shift along
Note this now, it explains a lot later: the synthetic generator labels its fake proteins by family, not by EC. So for most of this project the synthetic side has been simulating homology recovery while the thesis's stated goal is function recovery. Closing that gap is what the August work was about.

2 · Embeddings

A protein language model (here ESM-C) reads an amino-acid sequence and outputs a list of 960 numbers. That list is the embedding. It's a summary of the protein in a form a computer can do arithmetic on.

The useful property: proteins that are similar (structurally, functionally, evolutionarily) end up with similar lists of numbers. So "similar protein" becomes "nearby point", and questions about biology become questions about geometry.

Think of each protein as a single dot floating in a 960-dimensional space. You can't picture 960 dimensions, and §3 is about why your intuition for 2 or 3 will actively mislead you. But every operation in this project is one of three things:

  • distance between two dots; how different are these proteins
  • direction from one dot to another; a vector, which way did we move
  • a centroid: the average position of all dots with the same label; "where family X lives"

Everything else is bookkeeping.

3 · Properties of 960-dimensional space

Your 3-D intuition is wrong in high dimensions in specific, exploitable ways. Two of them matter enormously here, and one of them caused a real bug in this project.

Random directions are nearly perpendicular, and it gets worse with dimension

Pick two random directions in D dimensions and measure the angle between them. In 2-D, any angle is about as likely as any other. Crank D up and watch the distribution collapse onto 90°.

distribution of cos(angle) between 4,000 random vector pairs

F8in-browser illustrationno dataRandom directions are nearly perpendicular
What it isA Monte-Carlo demonstration: sample random direction pairs in n dimensions, histogram their cosine.
DatasetNone: random vectors drawn in your browser.
Why it is hereIt is the reason the v2a generator failed: independent per-family displacement inflates every gap by √(g²+2m²), +56% at the distances used, which drove the measured ceiling to 1.00. See §11.
ProvenanceLive simulation. The +56% figure it explains is measured, from the v2a run, not from this chart.
RelatedNothing; this is an illustration, not a run. See the catalogue for the experiments themselves.

Why this matters. At D=960 essentially every random direction is perpendicular to every other. So if you move two families by independent random vectors of length m, their displacement vectors are perpendicular, and the distance between them doesn't stay the same: it grows:

gap → √(gap² + 2m²) ← the Pythagorean blow-up when the two moves are perpendicular

At the distances used here that's a +56% inflation of the gaps between families. Families end up further apart than they started, the classification problem gets easier, and the "ceiling" you're measuring against shoots to 1.00. That's not a hypothetical; it's the v2a bug, one of three failed attempts documented in §11.

The second strangeness: almost all the variance is useless

Real ESM-C embeddings have 960 dimensions but an effective rank of 3–11. Meaning: although the data technically spans 960 directions, it's really only spread out along a handful of them. The rest is nearly flat.

And here's the part that broke the first generator: the directions with the most variance are not the directions that carry the label. Most of the spread is nuisance. This single fact is what §7 is about, and reproducing it is the central design achievement of v2.

Two facts to carry forward: (1) random directions are perpendicular, so independent moves inflate distances; (2) most variance carries no label information. Nearly every design decision in the generator is a response to one of these two.

How one measurement is made

Everything in this document is one of two numbers, produced by one procedure, run hundreds of times. This is that procedure, start to finish, before any statistic is defined on top of it.

Where a label comes from, on each side of the project

The classifier, the pool and the whole protocol are identical on both tracks. Only two things differ: where the 960 numbers come from, and what the label means. Follow the dashed line on each track — that is the label, and it is the part people expect to be computed and is not.

The consequence, stated once. On the real track the label is a chemical reaction, curated by a human. On the synthetic track it is an index standing for shared ancestry. The two tracks therefore answer different questions, and every synthetic number in this document is a homology result being read as if it spoke about function. That substitution is defensible — both axes turn out to be structured the same way — but it is a substitution.

Where the EC number comes from, and where source and target come from

"Transfer to organisms the model has never seen" sounds like two datasets. It is one. For the August run, every protein comes from ec_swissprot: 231,285 reviewed Swiss-Prot proteins. The cut is taxonomic:

SourceGammaproteobacteria, 64,791 proteins — the largest and best-studied group. The model is trained here.
TargetOne of 14 other groups: actinobacteria, euryarchaeota, streptophyta (plants), vertebrata, and so on. The model is tested here, having seen none of it.

So "train on well-studied bacteria, deploy on plants" is literally what happens, using one database split two ways. Each of the 14 targets is measured separately, which is why results come as fourteen numbers rather than one.

Two models, and only one of them was built here

Conflating these two is the easiest way to lose the plot:

ComponentWhat it doesTrained here?
ESM-C 300M A pretrained protein language model. Turns one amino-acid sequence into 960 numbers. It was trained by predicting hidden residues across millions of sequences and has never seen an EC number. Its output is computed once and cached to disk. frozen
The classifier The model built for this project: 960 → 512 → BatchNorm → ReLU → Dropout → 256 → ReLU → Dropout → K, 628,496 weights, Adam at learning rate 0.001. Takes the 960 numbers and predicts EC level 3. yes

Everything measured here is a property of the small classifier sitting on top of frozen embeddings. The language model is a fixed lens, not a participant.

The budget, and the one thing allowed to vary

Hand-labelling a protein means lab work, so only P of them can be labelled. The question is not how many, it is what mix. The adaptation pool holds exactly P proteins, of which a fraction r come from the target and the rest from the source. At P = 500:

rfrom targetfrom sourcetotal
0.00500500
0.3150350500
1.05000500
The total never moves. That is the whole design. If performance changes across that table, it changed because of composition and not because more data arrived. Every recovery curve in this document is a sweep across those rows.

The loop, in order

For one source→target pair, at three random seeds (42, 43, 44):

  1. Train the classifier on source embeddings. This is the source model.
  2. Score it on held-out target proteins with no adaptation at all. This is zero-shot: what transfer gives you free.
  3. Separately, train a fresh model on target data only. This is the ceiling: what is achievable ignoring transfer entirely.
  4. For each r on the grid 0, .05, .1, .2, .3, .5, .75, 1.0: assemble the pool, warm start from the source model's weights rather than from scratch, train on the pool, and score on held-out target.
  5. That sweep is the recovery curve. Read the two numbers off it.
retention = zero-shot ÷ ceiling. The share of achievable performance kept before labelling anything. No threshold, no grid, no bar — which is why it turned out to be the stable one.
r* = the smallest r whose seed-averaged final macro-F1 reaches 0.9 × ceiling. Average the seeds first, then threshold; the other order changes 28 of 55 cells.

How the recovery threshold is measured, in every generation

The protocol is identical for synthetic and real data. Only the source of the embeddings and the label axis change. The labelling budget is held fixed; only its composition varies.

The synthetic generator does not make EC numbers

This is worth being blunt about, because the name "synthetic data pipeline" suggests fake proteins and it is not that. The generator produces points in 960-dimensional space, drawn from families, and the label attached to a point is which family it was drawn from — an index. No sequence, no chemistry, no enzyme.

It exists because real biology will not let you turn a dial. You cannot ask for organisms "1.4 units away"; you get whatever the tree of life provides. The generator gives a distance knob d that can be swept smoothly, with the true answer known by construction.

The protocol above is identical for synthetic and for real data. Only two things change: where the 960 numbers come from (the generator, or frozen ESM-C on a real sequence), and what the label means (a family index, or an EC number).
And that second difference is the project's largest open problem. A family index is a homology label, so every synthetic result here is a homology recovery threshold being used to reason about a function problem. Building an EC-like label space was attempted and hit an unresolved purity-versus-coverage conflict (§13).

Which arm used which data

Three label axes appear in this document, for historical reasons: until August the pipeline could only produce homology labels. When reading any figure, its stamp names which of these it is.

4 · The recovery threshold and the dip

Setup. You have a model trained on source proteins. You want it to work on target proteins from somewhere new. You can afford to hand-label a fixed number of proteins: call that number P, the budget. Labelling means real lab work, so P is small.

The question isn't "should I get more data" (obviously yes). It's: given that I can only label P proteins, what fraction of them should be from the new place? Call that fraction r. The total is always P, only the mix changes.

rtarget proteinssource proteinstotal
0.00500500
0.3150350500
1.05000500

r\* is the smallest r that gets you to 90% of a target bar. That's it. That's the whole statistic.

Careful: this definition replaced an earlier one, silently. In June, r* meant "the smallest r at which the dip appears". From mid-July it means "the smallest r that recovers to 90% of the ceiling". Both are called r* in the notes. Every number you'll be asked about uses the second. The switch also introduced the dependency on a ceiling, which is where nearly every later error came from.

The dip: why this isn't trivial

Naively, feeding the model a few correct target examples should help a little. It doesn't. It often makes things worse first. That's negative transfer, and it's the phenomenon the whole pipeline was built to reproduce.

Why it happens: the source-trained model has drawn a decision boundary that is optimal for source data. In the target region that boundary is in the wrong place. A handful of target examples is enough to disturb the model's existing solution but not enough to replace it, so you break what worked without yet building what will.

Drag the distance. The curve is target performance as the mix r goes from all-source to all-target. Note that at larger distances the left end sits below the starting point: that's the dip.

The chart above cannot show you negative transfer, and if you went looking for it there you were right not to find it. Every dot is the score at the end of an adaptation run. What a dip actually is

Adaptation is a training run, so it has a during. The model starts at its zero-shot score, and while it learns the new pool it first gets worse, bottoms out, and then climbs back. Three numbers are recorded for every run — where it started, the worst it got, and where it finished — and dip depth is the gap between the first two.

Relatedjob 47292627: the real EC ladder · job 47136848: the v2 sweep
On real data the dip is unmistakable. At r = 0 every group falls 0.10 to 0.30 below where it started. Feed in target data and the dip shrinks monotonically to nothing by about r = 0.5. That is negative transfer, and it is exactly the phenomenon the thesis is named after.
On synthetic data it essentially isn't there, and it is a real limitation. The largest synthetic dips (0.055–0.084) occur at d = 0.00, where there is no shift at all, so they are the noise floor. At d = 0.5 the dip is 0.075, the same size as the floor. By d ≥ 1.0 it is zero, because zero-shot has already collapsed to 0.08 and there is nothing left to fall from.

So the generator that was built specifically to make negative transfer possible produces far less of it than reality does. The v0 → v1 rebuild (§12) fixed "structurally impossible"; it did not get to "quantitatively realistic". Nothing in the notes claims otherwise, but nothing flags it either, and it is the kind of omission a reader is likely to notice.

Read the left-hand end carefully: it is the control, not the result

At r = 0 the pool contains no target proteins at all. It is 1,000 more proteins from the source; the distribution the model was already trained on. Yet the curve usually starts below the zero-shot line, meaning that extra training made the model worse.

dzero-shotafter adapting at r = 0change
0.000.85210.8014−0.051
0.250.76310.7515−0.012
0.500.54560.5139−0.032
0.750.26590.2656−0.000
1.000.07820.0874+0.009
Note the top row. The biggest drop happens at d = 0.00; where there is no shift at all. Source and target are the same world, nothing has moved, and it still loses 5 points. So this is not negative transfer. It is the noise floor of the procedure itself: 32 gradient steps, each estimated from only 32 randomly-drawn proteins, at a learning rate tuned for training a fresh model; applied to one that had already settled. You are jostling something that was balanced, and 32 steps is not enough to settle back.

That is precisely why r = 0 is in the design. It is the control condition: how much damage does any extra training do, regardless of where the data came from? A drop at r > 0 only counts as domain shift if it is bigger than the r = 0 drop. The June notes measured this floor at about 0.09 and concluded that only the r = 0.10 dip was cleanly above it; everything else was inside the wobble.

Two different things get called "the dip", and it is worth keeping them apart.
  • The dip over adaptation steps; performance falls, then climbs, as training proceeds. This is the real negative-transfer signature, and it is what §D shows live.
  • The left end of this curve sitting low: a different axis entirely (pool composition, not time), and mostly the noise floor above.
The trap that r* has always been vulnerable to: r* is a fraction measured against a bar. If the bar moves for reasons that have nothing to do with the shift, r* changes and you conclude something false about biology. Different versions of this mistake appear in §11, §12 and §16; it is genuinely the recurring theme of the whole project.

5 · Why synthetic data is required

You have real proteins. Why simulate?

What you needReal dataSynthetic
Vary distance smoothly❌ nature gives you fixed groups at fixed distances, awkwardly clustered✅ it's a slider
Hold task difficulty constant❌ every group has its own difficulty✅ by construction (§11)
Know the ground truth of the shift❌ you can only estimate it✅ you wrote it
Unlimited samples❌ insecta has 1,970 proteins, full stop✅ generate more
Go beyond what exists❌ nothing on Earth is further than the furthest thing on Earth✅ set d = 2.0
Be actually true✅❌ only as true as its calibration

The intended workflow is a loop: measure real geometry → set the fake knobs to match → verify the fake data behaves like the real data → then use the fake data to explore regimes reality doesn't offer.

The second-to-last step is the one that earns the whole thing its keep, and it's the step the August EC run put under real strain (§16).

← Overview Generator v0 →

The argument

Generator v0

The oracle-labelled generator, and why it could not produce negative transfer

The first generator. It labelled every point (source and target alike) with one frozen random network called the oracle, and its shift knob only tightened the source. Both choices are individually reasonable and jointly fatal: together they make the phenomenon under study structurally impossible.

The oracle is not in the current pipeline. It was a component of v0, it was deliberately removed in v1 as a bug fix, and neither v1 nor v2 uses it. It came back in August as an investigation; could a random network manufacture an EC-like label space?, and that investigation is unresolved. If someone says “the oracle generates the synthetic labels” that was true in June and has been false since.

How v0 built its data, and why the dip was impossible

One universe, one labeller, and a shift knob that only tightened the source. Both choices are individually reasonable; together they remove the phenomenon the project set out to measure.

Why v0 could not produce a dip

This explains what the oracle was for, and why it was removed. In v0, one frozen random network assigned labels to every point, source and target alike. So the true labelling rule P(y|x) was identical everywhere in space. A source-trained model was never wrong on the target, only less certain. And the "shift" knob made the source tighter around the same centroids, so the target was a strict superset of the source region.

Under those two conditions, negative transfer is structurally impossible. You can crank the shift arbitrarily high and never see a dip. The pipeline was producing exactly the null result its construction guaranteed.

13 · The oracle, and its removal

A common misconception. The oracle is not part of the current pipeline. It was a component of v0, it was deliberately removed in v1 as a bug fix, and neither v1 nor v2 uses it. If someone tells you "the oracle generates the synthetic labels", that was true in June and has been false since.

What it was

A randomly initialised neural network, never trained. You feed it a point, it outputs a score per class, and the highest score is that point's label. The appeal: it manufactures a labelling rule that is deterministic, consistent, and arbitrary: no biology needed.

Why it had to go

Precisely because it was too consistent. One global oracle means one global P(y|x), which means the source model is never actually wrong on the target, which means no negative transfer, which was the phenomenon under study. v1's fix was blunt: delete the oracle, and make the label simply which family did I draw this point from.

v1 and v2: y = family index ← the label is just the cluster you were sampled from

Why it came back in August, and what it's for now

Here's the tension. In v1/v2 the label is the family. But a family is a Pfam-like concept: ancestry. The thesis is about EC: function. So the synthetic side has been simulating homology recovery while claiming to inform function recovery.

The August investigation (oracle_label_space.py) asked: could a random-network oracle, applied on top of the family structure, manufacture a label space that looks like EC rather than Pfam? If yes, the synthetic side could finally simulate the right thing.

Three measurements define "looks like EC", comparing EC labels against Pfam labels on real data:

QuantityMeansReal value
puritywithin one family, what fraction of proteins share the most common EC69.3%
promiscuityfraction of families containing more than one EC100%
coveragehow many families does one EC class span2.98

What was learned: including two negative results

  • The scale knob was completely inert. The oracle applies LayerNorm after every hidden layer, and LayerNorm removes any overall scaling of its input. So multiplying the input by a constant cannot change which output is largest. Scales from 0.25 to 4.0 gave byte-identical label spaces. Any earlier tuning over that knob was a no-op.
  • The oracle's labels were nearly independent of family, and that was the bug. It reads the full 960-d vector, which is mostly nuisance by construction, so a random network slices along directions carrying no family information. Real function is not independent of homology. Adding a signal_weight knob that tilts the oracle's input toward the signal subspace lifted purity from 33% to 67%: right at the real 69.3%.
  • But purity and coverage cannot be satisfied at once. 20 classes gives purity 66.8% ✓ but coverage 8.32 ✗. 200 classes gives coverage 4.72 (closest) but purity 39.3% ✗. Real data wants 69% purity and 2.98 coverage simultaneously, which implies a heavy-tailed distribution of ECs within each family: one dominant EC plus a long tail. The oracle's argmax produces roughly balanced classes within a family, so it can only buy purity by having very few classes.
Status: unresolved. The proposed fix: give the oracle a Zipf-like label distribution within each family, not just across families; has not been implemented. So the synthetic side still labels by family, and the EC/Pfam gap on the synthetic side is still open.

What the oracle was tuned on, and the trade-off it exposed

Before it was removed, the oracle was tuned properly, and the tuning run is worth keeping because it exposed a constraint that is still unresolved. A 24-task job swept four network shapes against six values of the label-noise σ, scoring each resulting label space on three quantities:

QuantityMeans
puritywithin one family, what fraction of proteins share the most common label
promiscuityfraction of families containing more than one label
coveragehow many families one label class spans

The three-layer oracle 1024,1024,512 dominates all three two-layer shapes at every σ, giving higher purity and lower promiscuity at matched σ. Its full row:

σpurity %promiscuity % coverage
0.190.327.213.9
0.376.650.723.1
0.569.1 59.132.4
0.765.062.740.7
1.061.964.950.0
1.460.065.857.3

24-task Slurm array, jobs 46010737 and 46010738 (the dependent merge), 4 June 2026, n = 1,000,000 per universe. results/oracle_search/full_grid_results_test_run_01.csv. The highlighted row is pinned in configs/liam_master.yaml, template_master.yaml and parity_test.yaml, so it is load-bearing for everything v0 produced.

Purity and coverage move in strict opposition. At σ = 0.1 the label space is clean (90% purity) and badly spread (coverage 14). At σ = 1.4 it is well spread (coverage 57) and dirty (60% purity). No setting gives both, and no architecture escapes it.

Why that constraint still matters, four months later

The oracle came back in August as an investigation rather than a component: could a random network manufacture a label space that looks like EC rather than like Pfam? If it could, the synthetic side could finally simulate function recovery rather than homology recovery. The real targets were measured first, on the EC dataset:

Quantityreal (EC against Pfam) best oracle achievedratio
within-family purity0.6930.393 0.57
family promiscuity1.0001.0001.00
coverage2.9804.720 1.58

Best configuration found: 200 classes (125 actually used), hidden layers 256 and 128, signal_weight 0.99. Source: /scratch/lmk04992/ec_analysis/oracle_label_space.json, job 47270758, 4 Aug 2026 at 23:16. An earlier attempt, 47270580 at 23:13, was superseded and its output overwritten.

The same trade-off, in the same direction. Real data wants 69% purity and coverage 2.98 at the same time. That combination implies roughly 19 EC classes per Pfam of which one holds 69% of the members, which is a heavy-tailed within-family label distribution. The oracle's argmax produces roughly balanced classes within a family, so it can only buy purity by having very few classes. The proposed repair, giving the oracle a Zipf-like label distribution within each family rather than only across families, has not been implemented.
Two further findings from the same investigation. First, the scale knob was completely inert: the oracle applies LayerNorm after every hidden layer, and LayerNorm removes any overall scaling of its input, so scales from 0.25 to 4.0 produced byte-identical label spaces. Any earlier tuning over that knob was a no-op. Second, the oracle's labels were nearly independent of family, which was the actual bug: it reads the full 960-dimensional vector, which is mostly nuisance by construction, so a random network slices along directions carrying no family information. Adding signal_weight, which tilts the oracle's input toward the family-carrying subspace, lifted purity from 33% to 67%.
← The question Generator v1 →

The argument

Generator v1

The first recovery-threshold curve, and the moving ceiling that invalidated it

v1 deleted the oracle and made the label simply which family did I draw this point from. It displaced each target family toward another family’s position, so the source-trained boundary became genuinely wrong. It worked: the first recovery-threshold curve in the project came out of it, and it was the project's first reported result.

It was also invalid, for a reason not identified for eight days. The displacement contracted the whole centroid configuration at mid-distance, so the ceiling (the bar r* is scored against) moved with the distance knob. r* was being graded against a target that dipped exactly where the ceiling dipped.

How v1 built its shift, and how that moved the bar

The oracle is gone and the label is simply which family a point was drawn from. Each target family then slides a fraction d toward a different family's home, along a fixed derangement.

v1's ceiling was U-shaped in distance; the bar r* is scored against was itself moving

At d ≈ 0.5 every family sits at a midpoint and the whole configuration contracts by √((1−d)²+d²), classes overlap, and the ceiling craters. The effect on r*

Once the ceiling is realistic, the recovery threshold becomes undefined almost immediately; not because the shift is hard, but because the bar moved:

“never” = the adapted model does not reach 0.9 × ceiling at any mixing fraction, including r = 1.0. Same source files as above.

The write-up of these runs at the time said “confirmed robust: preserves the r*(d) law&rdquo. That sentence is defensible only if you read the first three rows and stop. Rows 4 onward are entirely censored, and the ceiling column (which was in the same CSV) is U-shaped. This is the same error class as August’s defect (d): censoring read as a property of the shift when it is a property of the bar.

How the ceiling bug went undiagnosed

On 14 July, a run measured v1's ceiling as 0.79 → 0.49 → 0.77 across distance. The U-shape was right there. It was explained away as a consequence of the families being crowded together, and the fix chosen was to un-crowd them, which pinned the ceiling at 1.0 and hid the symptom while leaving the confound intact.

Worse: two follow-up runs at wider spreads were written up as "confirmed robust: preserves the r*(d) law". On 22 July those same two runs turned out to be the evidence against it: their ceilings were predicted from centroid geometry alone at correlation 0.993 and 0.997. The confirmation and the refutation were the same two jobs.

This failure mode is worth stating explicitly. The question it invites is whether the current results make the same mistake. The honest answer is that the failure mode is now well understood, having been hit four separate times, and the current protocol reports three different ceilings next to every number precisely because of it.
← Generator v0 Generator v2 · design →

The argument

Generator v2 · design

How the current simulator is built, knob by knob

The current generator, built after v1 was traced back to its derangement. Everything on this page is design; how the fake universe is constructed and what each knob does. The results it produced are on the next page.

The central idea. Real embeddings do something that looks impossible: classes overlap heavily (gap ÷ σ ≈ 1) and are still easy to tell apart (F1 ≈ 0.90). The only structure that resolves that contradiction is a signal/nuisance split: a few directions that separate classes, and many carrying most of the spread and no class information at all. Every other design decision follows from it.

How v2 builds its shift, and why the bar stays put

The latent space is split in two before anything moves, and every family-specific motion is constrained to be an exact isometry of the centroid configuration.

6 · Constructing the synthetic universe

A "universe" is one fixed fake world: where each family lives, how spread out each is, how big each is. Source and target share the same universe; the target is the same world, shifted.

It's built once, in build_universe(). Here's the whole thing in order.

Step 1: a latent space, split in two

latent_dim = signal_dim + nuisance_dim ← default: 8 + 64 = 72

Two bundles of directions. Signal directions are where family identity lives. Nuisance directions carry variation that has nothing to do with the label. This split is the core idea of v2 and gets its own section (§7).

Step 2: place the family centroids

C = np.zeros((n_families, latent_dim))
C[:, :signal_dim] = rng.standard_normal((n_families, signal_dim)) * centroid_spread

Read that carefully: the centroids are zero everywhere except the signal dimensions. Each family's "home address" is a random point in the 8-dimensional signal subspace, and identically zero in all 64 nuisance dimensions. Families differ only in signal coordinates. That's what makes those directions "signal": it's true by construction.

Step 3: how spread out is each family

var[:signal_dim] = sigma_signal ** 2
lam = (np.arange(1, nuisance_dim + 1)) ** (-spectrum_exponent)
lam /= lam.sum()
var[signal_dim:] = lam * (nuisance_ratio * signal_dim * sigma_signal ** 2)

Signal dimensions get a modest, equal variance. Nuisance dimensions get a power-law spectrum; the first nuisance direction has a lot of variance, the second less, decaying as k−1.6, and the whole nuisance bundle is scaled to carry nuisance_ratio (≈3) times the total signal variance.

The power law is what produces the low effective rank measured in real data. The nuisance_ratio is what makes families overlap as heavily as real ones do.

Step 4: realistic messiness

fam_scale = exp(uniform(-s/2, s/2))     # families differ in tightness, real ratio ≈1.9
w = (1..n)^(-log(skew)/log(n))          # family sizes follow a power law, real skew ≈36×

Step 5: pre-draw the shift ingredients

U = dict(shared_sig = random unit vector inside the signal subspace,
         shared_nui = random unit vector inside the nuisance subspace,
         Q          = random orthogonal basis of the signal subspace,
         fam_nui    = per-family nuisance directions)

shared_sig and shared_nui are the two ingredients β mixes between (§10). Q is the basis the rotation happens in (§9, §11).

Step 6: project up to 960 dimensions

P = randn(latent_dim, 960) / √latent_dim    X = latent @ P

The real geometry lives in 72 latent dimensions; it then gets projected into the 960-dimensional ambient space to look like a real embedding. This projection is injective (no information is destroyed), so the difficulty of the classification problem is set entirely by the latent geometry. The 960 is cosmetic realism.

Step 7: measure the mean gap

mean_gap = average distance between all pairs of family centroids

This is the ruler. Every distance in the system is quoted in multiples of it, so results don't depend on arbitrary units.

7 · Signal and nuisance subspaces

Real embeddings have a property that sounds contradictory: families overlap heavily, yet classify almost perfectly.

Measured on real ESM-C data:

mean gap between families ÷ within-family spread ≈ 1.0 ← families are only about one "family-width" apart: massive overlap …and yet a classifier reaches F1 ≈ 0.90
Why the split was forced by a measurement, and where it sits against prior work568 words

Where this idea came from: it was forced, not chosen

This is worth setting out, because "why model it that way?" is a fair question and the answer here is unusually strong: the design was deduced from a contradiction in the measurements. Nobody sat down and preferred it.

Two numbers were measured on real embeddings in July, and they cannot both be true of round blobs (isotropic Gaussians). For round blobs, the best accuracy achievable is fixed by the gap-to-spread ratio and there is nothing you can do about it. That hard ceiling, simulated at the real settings: 16 classes, 960 dimensions, best-possible classification:

The impossible measurement

The curve is the best any round-blob model can ever achieve. The orange dot is where real protein embeddings actually sit. It is nowhere near the curve.

F19analyticreal datafamily labelsswissprot_esmc / _esm2 + taxonomy_ladder · ESM-C, ESM-2The impossible measurement: Bayes accuracy vs separation ratio
The curveAnalytic. Best achievable accuracy for an isotropic Gaussian mixture as a function of gap ÷ &sigma. No data, no model: a geometric bound.
The orange dotReal measurement. ESM-C embeddings sit at gap ÷ σ ≈ 1.0 while achieving macro-F1 ≈ 0.90: far above what the curve permits.
Where the dot comes fromsrc/measure_real_geometry.py over swissprot_esmc/, swissprot_esm2/ and the four taxonomy_ladder/ rungs, 22 Jul 2026. Pfam labels.
What it forcesReal embeddings cannot be round blobs. That contradiction is the whole argument for the signal/nuisance split: a forced conclusion, not a modelling preference.
Relatedthe real-geometry measurement

Read it off: at gap ÷ σ = 1.0 a round-blob model caps at 0.18. To reach 0.93 it needs a ratio near 5–6. Real data reports 1.0 and 0.90 at the same time: far above anything the curve permits.

The deduction, in one step

If the blobs overlap heavily and are easy to tell apart, the overlap and the separation cannot be happening in the same directions. So the blobs are not round: there must be some directions where classes separate cleanly, and other directions carrying most of the spread but no class information at all.

That is the signal/nuisance split. It's the minimal structure that resolves the contradiction: a forced conclusion, not a modelling preference.

What makes it convincing: it also explained something it was never fitted to. The same split independently reproduces the measured effective rank of 3–11 out of 960, because if most variance sits in a steeply-ranked power-law nuisance spectrum, the data is nearly flat in most directions. One structural change, two independent measurements accounted for. JULY22 puts it in a line: it "reproduces gap ≈ σ yet F1 ≈ 0.90 and low effective rank at once."
Be precise about what's novel here, because this is a likely place to get pushed. The concept (a discriminative subspace sitting inside a larger non-discriminative one) is completely standard. Fisher's linear discriminant analysis is literally between-class scatter versus within-class scatter; signal-versus-noise subspaces are routine in signal processing. Nobody will challenge the idea itself.

What is yours is the derivation from a specific measured contradiction in protein embeddings, and the calibration of the ratio to real data. If asked "why this model?", the strong answer isn't "it's standard": it's "we measured two quantities that are jointly impossible for an isotropic mixture, so we asked what the simplest structure permitting both would be."

What the split does, once you have it

v1's hidden cheat: it inflated family separation 6× to hit realistic accuracy. It looked right on the accuracy number while being wrong about the geometry: papering over the missing anisotropy.

The resolution: the overlap and the separability happen in different directions. Families are well separated along the 8 signal directions. They're hopelessly overlapping along the 64 nuisance directions. Since the nuisance directions carry ~3× more variance, the overall gap-to-spread ratio looks terrible, while a classifier that has learned to ignore nuisance directions does fine.

See it: one signal axis, one nuisance axis

Four families. Left panel: what you see if you plot a signal direction against a nuisance direction. Right panel: the two signal directions alone. Turn up the nuisance ratio and watch the left panel turn to mush while the right stays perfectly clean.

left: signal dim 1 × nuisance dim 1: right: signal dim 1 × signal dim 2

This is the single most important design decision in the generator. One change (splitting the space into a small label-carrying subspace and a large label-free subspace with a power-law spectrum) reproduces three real measurements at once: gap ≈ σ, F1 ≈ 0.90, and effective rank in the single digits.

8 · The shift: d, α and β

Now the target. The target universe is the source universe with every family moved. The move is described by three numbers.

d: how far

m_total = d × d_unit_gaps × mean_gap d_unit_gaps = 1.20 by default, so d=1.0 means "move 1.2 mean-gaps"

The units are chosen so that d = 1.0 equals the real bacteria→plants shift. That's why the sweep goes to d = 2.0: twice as far as crossing from bacteria to plants.

First: what "shared" and "differential" actually mean

This term gets used constantly and is never defined. Here it is.

When you go from source to target, every class moves. Class 1 moves from where it was to somewhere new; class 2 moves; and so on. So you have one arrow per class: its displacement vector, just "from where it was, to where it now is".

Now ask the only interesting question about a pile of arrows: what do they have in common?

average all the arrows together → that common part is the SHARED component subtract that average from each → what's left over is the DIFFERENTIAL component
The flock-of-birds picture. A flock flies north. Every bird's motion = the flock moving north (shared by all of them) + that individual bird's wobble relative to the flock (different for each).

Shared = the flock's movement. Every class moves by this much, in this direction, together.
Differential = each class's own wobble on top.

α is just: how much of the total motion is the flock moving, versus the birds wobbling? α = 1 → a perfectly rigid flock, no wobble. α = 0 → the flock's centre doesn't move at all, it's pure wobble.

Why this distinction is the whole point:

  • A shared move doesn't change the classes' arrangement relative to each other. The whole constellation slides. Class 3 is still the same distance from class 7. A model just needs to know "everything shifted that way".
  • A differential move rearranges them. Class 3 and class 7 are now differently positioned relative to each other, so the boundary the source model learned between them is in genuinely the wrong place.

That's why α = 1 is called covariate shift and α = 0 is called concept shift, and why the sliders in §9 show a translation at one end and a rotation at the other.

One naming trap. The differential component is also called the family-specific part, and in the code the shared part is the shared translation. Three names, two things: shared = shared translation = the flock; differential = family-specific = the wobble.

α: does everything move together?

Total movement splits into those two parts, and α sets how the squared length divides:

m_shared = m_total × √α everyone moves the same way m_family = m_total × √(1 − α) each family moves its own way

Because it's a squared-length split, α has a direct interpretation you can measure in real data: α equals the expected cosine between two families' shift vectors.

  • α = 1: pure covariate shift. The entire cloud slides rigidly. All families keep their relative positions perfectly.
  • α = 0: pure concept shift. Families rearrange relative to each other. The decision boundary the source model learned is now genuinely in the wrong place.

Real data measures α between 0.41 and 0.70, mostly-shared with a real idiosyncratic component.

The whole shift, at a glance

Two knobs, applied in two steps. This is the entire shift model:

STEP 1: α splits the total move total move → shared the flock going north + differential each class's own wobble STEP 2: β splits the shared part only shared move → signal part √β ← directions that matter for the label + nuisance part √(1−β) ← directions the classifier ignores differential → always 100% signal. β gets no say here.
Read it as one sentence: α decides how much of the move is everyone together versus each class separately; β then decides, of the together-part only, how much runs along directions that actually matter for telling classes apart.

So the signal fraction of the whole shift is (1 − α) + α·β, not β.
Why the wobble doesn't get a β; this is a real design constraint, not an oversight. Class centroids have zero nuisance component to begin with; they live only in signal dimensions. If each class were given a different nuisance offset, the nuisance directions would suddenly carry class information; they'd stop being nuisance, the classifier would find that new structure, and the ceiling jumps to 1.00 (measured). A single common nuisance offset is safe precisely because it creates no differences between classes.

β: does the move damage function?

β applies only to the shared component, and splits its direction between the signal subspace and the nuisance subspace:

u = √β · shared_sig + √(1−β) · shared_nui M = M + m_shared · u / ‖u‖
  • β = 1: the common translation runs entirely along label-carrying directions.
  • β = 0; it runs entirely along directions the classifier ignores; it should be harmless.
Why β exists at all. On the real ladder, archaea and plants sit at almost identical shift distances (1.16 vs 1.20 mean-gaps) but have very different zero-shot performance (0.85 vs 0.61). Distance alone can't explain that. β was introduced as the extra explanatory variable: taxonomy moves embeddings partly in directions that don't matter for function.
Two things about β that the code's own help text gets wrong: noted because they are easy to misread.

The --beta flag says "fraction of the shift lying in the signal subspace". That is not what it does. β governs only the shared translation. The family-specific part is 100% inside the signal subspace by construction. So the true signal fraction of the whole shift is:

signal fraction = (1 − α) + α·β

Consequences you can check on the sliders below:

  • At α = 0, β does nothing at all; there is no shared translation for it to steer.
  • At α = 1, the rotation does nothing; the entire move is the shared translation.
Flag for later (§17): β behaves in the generator exactly as designed; turn it up, damage goes up. On real data it does the opposite. That contradiction is unresolved and is one of the sharper open questions here.

Where these knobs come from: the shift measured on real embeddings

d, α and β are not free parameters. Each was set from a measurement on real ESM-C embeddings, and the two figures below are those measurements. They are from 4 August, on the 5-domain dataset with EC labels; the 6 August rebuild reproduced both at 11 times the scale.

9 · The α knob

Watch the target configuration move

Grey = where families sit in the source. Blue = where they sit in the target. This runs the real construction: a rigid translation for the shared part, and a rotation of the whole configuration for the family-specific part.

F23in-browser illustrationfamily labelsα, interactively: watch the target configuration move
What it isThe v2 generator’s shift maths, run live on 6 classes in 2-D as you drag α and d.
DatasetNone. Class centroids are generated in the page; the rule applied to them is the real one.
The rule shownshift = α-weighted shared translation + (1−α)-weighted family-specific rotation, both isometries (§11).
