Push d past ~1.1 with α at 0 and the picture stops moving. That is real, and it is worth understanding. The family-specific part is a rotation, and a rotation can only go to 180°; a point reflection, where every centroid has been flipped straight through the origin. Past that it comes back toward where it started, so 180° is the furthest anything can ever get.

That caps family-specific displacement at √2 ≈ 1.4 mean-gaps, permanently, whatever you set d to:
αd at which the rotation saturates
0.001.13
0.251.30
0.501.60
0.752.26
At α = 0 it stops completely, because there is no shared translation left to keep growing. At higher α the rotation still freezes but the constellation keeps sliding, so it does not look stuck.
And this has a real consequence for reading any plot at large d. Past saturation the total movement grows more slowly than d suggests, and its character silently changes, from "rotation plus translation" to "almost pure translation". So the sweep's points at d = 1.5 and d = 2.0 are not "the d = 1.0 shift, only further". They are an increasingly pure covariate shift, because the concept-shift component has hit its ceiling.

It is also a hard design limit: you cannot build an arbitrarily large concept shift out of a rotation. Doing so would need a different isometry, and finding one that isn't a rotation while still preserving every pairwise distance is exactly the constraint §11 is about.

Two things to try:

  • Set α = 1. The whole constellation slides without changing shape. Every pairwise distance is identical. The target problem is exactly as hard as the source problem, but the source model's boundary is now in the wrong place.
  • Set α = 0. The constellation rotates. Families swap neighbourhoods. Crucially the shape still doesn't change: check the "mean gap" readout, it doesn't move.
Why rotation and not "give each family a random push"? Because of §3: random pushes in high dimensions are perpendicular, which would inflate all the gaps and make the target problem easier. A rotation is an isometry (it preserves every distance exactly), so families can move arbitrarily far while the problem stays exactly as hard. This is the design idea the generator is proudest of, and §11 is the story of learning it the hard way.

Two facts about the rotation that are easy to miss

Families don't all move the same distance. The displacement from a rotation is

‖R(θ)c − c‖ = 2·sin(θ/2)·‖c‖ ← proportional to how far the family already sat from the centre

So the requested magnitude is matched only on average. Families far from the origin of the signal subspace move further than families near it.

The rotation saturates. θ can only go to π (a point reflection: everything flipped through the origin). Past that a rotation starts coming back around. That caps the family-specific displacement at about 1.4 mean-gaps. Beyond that point, only the shared translation keeps growing with d, so at large d the total movement grows more slowly than d suggests. This should be borne in mind when reading any plot at d = 1.5 or 2.0.

10 · The β knob

How β is built, and why there are square roots

The generator makes the shared direction by mixing two ingredients: one random unit vector living in the signal subspace, one in the nuisance subspace. β sets the recipe. The squares are the point: drag β and watch their areas.

F24in-browser illustrationno dataHow β is built, and why there are square roots
What it isA live construction of the β split: how a shift of fixed length is divided between the signal subspace and its complement.
DatasetNone.
Definition shownβ = ‖P_B(v)‖² ÷ ‖v‖² a squared-length fraction, which is where the square roots come from.
ProvenanceIllustration of a definition.
RelatedNothing; this is an illustration, not a run. See the catalogue for the experiments themselves.
Why √β and not β? Because β is defined as a fraction of squared length, and the two ingredients are perpendicular, so Pythagoras applies:
u = √β · signal_direction + √(1−β) · nuisance_direction ‖u‖² = (√β)² + (√(1−β))² = β + (1−β) = 1 ✓ always a unit vector squared length in signal = β ✓ exactly what we wanted
Weighting by the square roots is what makes the squared split come out exactly right. If you weighted by β and (1−β) directly, neither identity would hold. Same reason α uses √α and √(1−α) in §8; it is a squared-length split too.

The plane shown is one signal direction (horizontal) against one nuisance direction (vertical). The arrow is the shared translation. β decides how much of it lies along the signal axis: the axis that actually separates the families.

The three conflicting claims about β, reconciled1062 words

Is β a signal/nuisance split? Resolving the conflict

Three different claims get tangled here and they pull in opposite directions. Taken one at a time, none of them is mysterious.

Claim 1: "β is a signal/nuisance split" · TRUE

In the generator, β does precisely what the name says. It mixes one direction drawn from the signal subspace with one drawn from the nuisance subspace:

u = √β · shared_sig + √(1−β) · shared_nui

And it behaves exactly as designed. Measured in the v2 sweep: β = 0.05 → zero-shot 0.705; β = 0.50 → zero-shot 0.399. Turn β up, damage goes up. If this is your mental model, it is correct.

Claim 2: "β doesn't cover the whole shift" · TRUE, but a separate point

β steers only the shared translation. The family-specific part is 100% signal by construction, so the total signal fraction of the shift is (1−α) + αβ. This is a footnote about which piece β controls. It has nothing to do with whether β is a signal/nuisance split; it is one; it just isn't applied to everything.

Claim 3: "β behaves backwards" · TRUE, and only on real data

This is the one that creates the confusion, because there are two different βs:

Synthetic βReal β
What it isa knob you seta quantity you measure
Signal subspacedeclared: you built itestimated by SVD of the EC centroids
Behaviour↑β → ↑damage, as intended↑β → ↓damage, backwards

Why they disagree: one number explains it

In the generator, every signal direction has identical variance (var[:signal_dim] = sigma_signal²). Moving one unit along signal direction 3 does exactly as much damage as one unit along direction 7. There is no confound.

On real data, B is built by SVD, keeping the directions with the most between-class spread, which selects for wide directions by construction. Measured on gammaproteobacteria (167 EC centroids, B = top 22 of 960):

Direction in Bspread of centroids along it× narrower than the 1st
1st0.1761.0×
2nd0.0782.2×
6th0.0394.5×
22nd0.01611.3×
The widest direction in the real function subspace is 11.3× wider than the narrowest. In the generator that ratio is exactly 1.0.

So on real data "inside B" mostly means "along a roomy axis", and moving one Euclidean unit along a roomy axis barely changes which class you resemble, because the classes are spread far apart there. One unit along a cramped axis throws you past several classes.

β was meant to measure how function-damaging the move was. On real data it accidentally measures how much elbow room the move had, which is the opposite. Hence higher β → less damage.

Consistent supporting evidence: displacement outside B predicts damage nearly twice as strongly (ρ = −0.595) as displacement inside it (ρ = −0.367). Exactly what you'd expect if B is the roomy half of the space.

The proposed fix: whitening: what that actually means

Raw distance treats every direction as equivalent. Data doesn't. Describe people by height in cm and income in dollars, and "100 units of movement" is a whole metre of height or one hundred dollars of income. Euclidean distance calls those the same. Obviously wrong.

That is exactly what is happening to β. Moving 0.1 raw units:

Move of 0.1 raw units…in raw unitsin units of that direction's own spread
along direction 1 of B (spread 0.176)0.10.57: barely moved
along direction 22 of B (spread 0.016)0.16.25: flew past several classes

Whitening divides every direction by its own standard deviation:

whitened coordinate = raw coordinate ÷ (spread along that direction)

Afterwards the data has spread 1 along every direction, so "one unit" means "one standard deviation of the data here": the same thing everywhere. It is the z-score idea ((x − mean) / sd) generalised from one variable to every direction at once. The name comes from the result: spread becomes flat in all directions, like white noise having a flat spectrum.

Why this is the right fix, and why it is a real test rather than a patch. After whitening, "roominess" no longer exists; every direction is equally roomy by construction. So β can only measure the thing it was meant to: was the move along directions that distinguish classes, or not?

If whitened β comes out negative against retained F1, the original intuition was right all along and the raw definition was simply badly scaled. If it still comes out positive, then something real is happening that nobody has understood, and β should be dropped rather than defended. Either outcome is informative. Not yet run; it is a contained change to measure_ec_geometry.py and has been on the list since Aug 6.
Stated in one sentence: "β works in the simulation because we built the signal subspace to be isotropic; it fails on real data because the estimated function subspace is ordered by variance, so β ends up confounded with how wide the direction travelled is, by a factor of 11."
A further subtlety, on why β is confined to the shared translation. β applies only to the shared translation, never to the family-specific part. The generator's comments explain why: centroids have no nuisance component to begin with (§6, step 2). If each family were displaced by a different nuisance vector, then the nuisance subspace would suddenly carry label information (it would stop being nuisance), and the ceiling jumps to 1.00. A single common offset creates no such structure, so β is safe there and only there.

How β was tested, and why the answer reversed

Everything above describes what β is. This section is the experiment that asked what it does, on real embeddings, and it is worth following in detail because the conclusion flipped twice and the reason it flipped is a property of the control, not of β.

The injection experiment

Take real gammaproteobacterial embeddings. Choose a displacement of a fixed length, split that length between the function subspace B and its complement in the ratio β, apply it, and measure how much of the classifier's macro-F1 survives. Sweeping β at a fixed length asks the one question the observational data cannot answer: does moving along function directions cost more than moving the same distance elsewhere?

Only the last row is a fair test, and the first row is what was reported in August. Under the isotropic control the in-subspace half of the displacement is drawn from within B, which is a subspace estimated from the data, while the off-subspace half is drawn uniformly over all 960 dimensions, most of which the data never occupies. That contrast is a typical direction against an atypical one, not inside B against outside B. Once both halves come from the same distribution, the sign reverses.

Two honest qualifications on the shared arm. Its rise is monotone at 1 and 2 gaps only if you read the endpoints: there is a dip at β = 0.25 for one gap (0.698 then 0.679) and at β = 0.5 for two gaps (0.203 then 0.181). And its standard deviations across seeds are large relative to the effect, 0.07 to 0.23 at two gaps. The differential arm is fully monotone with standard deviations of 0.018 to 0.044, so it is the arm to quote.
What this leaves β as. B is built by SVD keeping the directions with the most between-class spread, which selects wide directions by construction. On the real data the widest direction in B is 11.3× the narrowest; in the generator every signal direction has identical width by construction. So on real data, “inside B” largely means “along a roomy axis”, and one Euclidean unit along a roomy axis barely changes which class a point resembles. β measures how much elbow room the move had, not how function-damaging it was. The proposed repair, defining β and magnitude in whitened units, has not been run.
Consistent with all of this: displacement outside B predicts damage roughly twice as strongly (ρ = −0.595) as displacement inside it (ρ = −0.367), over the 210 observational pairs. And β itself correlates with retained F1 at +0.280 (p = 0.0065), which has the wrong sign for a damage measure.

11 · The isometry rule, and three failed constructions

The rule: the target task must be exactly as hard as the source task. Otherwise r* confounds "how far did it move" with "how hard did it happen to get".

This project got it wrong three separate times. All three are documented in the generator's own docstring, which documents all three failures directly.

✗ v1: interpolate toward a shuffle

Move family f toward another family's position: M_f = (1−d)·C_f + d·C_π(f)

At d=1 you've just permuted the same points: same shape, same difficulty. At d≈0.5 every family sits at a midpoint, and the whole configuration contracts by √((1−d)²+d²).

Result: a U-shaped ceiling. The task got dramatically easier at the ends and harder in the middle, for purely geometric reasons. 21-point swing.

✗ v2a: push each family randomly

Give every family an independent random displacement of length m.

In high dimensions those are all perpendicular (§3), so gaps inflate: g → √(g² + 2m²), about +56% at d=1.

Result: the target problem got easier the further you moved. Ceiling pinned at 1.00 for every d > 0.

✗ v2b: interpolate toward a fresh draw

Blend the centroids toward a brand-new random set with √ weights. This preserves the distribution of configurations.

But not the realisation: with only 16 families, the particular fresh draw happened to be more separable.

Result: ceiling drifted 0.90 → 0.95. Subtler, still fatal.

✓ v2: rotate

Rotate the entire centroid configuration inside the signal subspace: M = C · R(θ)ᵀ

A rotation is an exact isometry. Every pairwise distance preserved to 1.8e-15: machine precision.

Result: families relocate arbitrarily far with provably zero change in difficulty. θ saturates at π (a point reflection), capping family-specific movement at ≈1.4 mean-gaps.

Compare all four constructions

Same starting configuration, four different ways of moving it. Watch the mean gap readout: that's the proxy for task difficulty. Only rotation holds it fixed.

F28in-browser illustrationfamily labelsfour constructions comparedCompare all four constructions: the isometry rule
What it isThe same starting configuration moved four different ways, with the mean gap (the proxy for task difficulty) read out live.
DatasetNone: live geometry in 2-D.
What each panel reproducesv1 (interpolate toward a derangement), v2a (independent random displacement), v2b (interpolate toward a fresh draw), v2c (rotate in the signal subspace: the one kept).
Real consequences of eachv1: 21-point ceiling swing. v2a: ceiling → 1.00. v2b: ceiling drifted 0.90 → 0.95. v2c: mean gap 10.15 / min gap 3.53 hold to all digits, Bayes ceiling 0.897–0.901. Those four are measured; this chart is the illustration of why.
ProvenanceIllustration. Numbers quoted above come from the v1/v2 sweeps (docs/notes/JULY22.md §3).
Relatedthe three failed constructions

After all that, exactly one knob is allowed to move the ceiling, deliberately: target_sigma_inflate, which widens within-family spread by (1 + inflate·d). It models the idea that a genuinely novel clade is intrinsically messier. It's set to 0.15 to reproduce the real ladder's mild 0.90 → 0.83 decline: a calibrated choice rather than a geometric accident.

Signal and nuisance, tested on real embeddings

Everything above treats the signal/nuisance split as a design choice: the generator declares a small subspace to carry the label and a large one to carry variance without it. This section asks whether real embeddings are built that way, and it was run on 12 August in response to the question: if data is shifted along the homology subspace, what does that do to function prediction?

Real embeddings allow the question to be asked properly, because they carry two label axes on the same points:

H = the directions along which Pfam families separate homology B = the directions along which EC classes separate function

If H and B were orthogonal, homology and function would be independently readable and a shift along H would leave function prediction untouched. If B sits inside H, an EC probe is largely reading homology and any homology-directed shift damages it.

How the homology / function subspace experiment was run

Two label axes exist on the same real embeddings, so there are two candidate signal subspaces. The experiment measures how much they overlap, whether either is necessary, and what happens when data is displaced along one but not the other.

Both subspaces are the top directions of the class-centroid cloud holding 90% of between-class variance, computed independently within each taxonomic group.

Between 83% and 91% of the EC between-class variance lies inside the Pfam subspace, in a bacterium, a firmicute, a plant and a vertebrate alike. The principal angles between the two subspaces have mean cosine 0.80 to 0.94 against random-subspace nulls of 0.11 to 0.22. These are not two subspaces. They are very nearly one subspace.

That is a geometric restatement of the homology confound already measured on the EC page: a Pfam-to-EC lookup table with no model in it scores 0.36 to 0.94, and the Pfam by EC centroid grid is 99.4% additive with Pfam alone explaining 95.6%. The subspace measurement says the same thing in the embedding's own coordinates.

In raw coordinates, deleting the function subspace does not cost anything. EC prediction goes 0.969 to 0.971, 0.980 to 0.981, 0.889 to 0.893, 0.946 to 0.956. In whitened coordinates the same deletion is catastrophic. EC prediction falls to 0.632, 0.667, 0.570 and 0.495. Four out of four. The subspace that carries the label is the whitened one, not the raw-variance one, and the difference between them is the entire content of the β paradox.

The causal version. Apply a displacement of fixed length, drawn from the data covariance so that the control is matched, restricted to one subspace at a time. The probe is never retrained, so this measures damage rather than adaptation. Retained EC macro-F1 at a displacement of two EC gaps:

The row that matters is “outside both”. In raw coordinates, displacing along directions that lie outside both label subspaces still destroys EC prediction: 0.159, 0.427, 0.105, 0.095 retained. Damage is diffuse, and the label subspaces are not special. In whitened coordinates the same displacement is almost harmless: 0.994, 0.999, 0.966, 0.964. Damage has become concentrated exactly where the labels live.

Whitening is what makes the signal/nuisance abstraction true. In the coordinates the project has always worked in, it is not.
What the random control establishes, and what it does not. Random subspaces of matched dimension are much less damaging than the structured ones in three of four domains (firmicutes is the exception), so the effect is about which directions, not merely how many. But the ordering among the structured conditions is not stable: H-not-B is worst in gammaproteobacteria and streptophyta, B-not-H is worst in firmicutes and vertebrata. Do not quote an ordering. Quote the raw-versus-whitened contrast, which is four out of four.
One thing that cannot be compared across the two coordinate systems. The magnitude normaliser is the mean pairwise EC-centroid distance, and it is 0.298 in raw coordinates against 23.09 in whitened ones. “Two gaps” is therefore not the same perturbation in the two spaces, and the absolute retained values are not comparable across the raw and whitened rows. What is comparable is the ordering of conditions within each row block, and the ablation in Result 2, which has no magnitude in it at all.

The answer to the question that prompted this

Shifting data along the homology subspace damages function prediction, and it is not possible to avoid it. Ninety percent of the EC between-class variance sits inside the Pfam subspace, so a homology-directed move is a function-directed move. In whitened coordinates, deleting the homology directions costs EC prediction as much as deleting the function directions does (0.706, 0.654, 0.399, 0.549 against 0.632, 0.667, 0.570, 0.495). In ESM-C, the two axes are not separable.
What this means for the generator. v2 assumes a small signal subspace that carries the label and a large nuisance subspace that does not, with both declared in advance and the signal directions of equal width. Real embeddings do not have that structure in raw coordinates: the label is redundant across many directions, and deleting the widest label-bearing ones costs nothing. They approximately do have it in whitened coordinates. The generator is a model of whitened embeddings, and it has always been compared against raw ones.
Limits of this experiment, stated plainly. One protein language model, so nothing here separates a property of ESM-C from a property of proteins; repeating it on ESM-2 is the obvious next step and was not run. One label level (EC level 3) and one probe (multinomial logistic regression); a non-linear head might read the raw subspaces differently. Four domains, chosen to span the tree, not sampled at random. And the vertebrata row rests on 7,727 proteins against 20,000 for the others.

Is any of this a property of ESM-C? The two-model replication

The largest interpretive risk in this project has been that ESM-C is the strongest taxonomic classifier of any protein language model tested, so a taxonomic-transfer result measured in ESM-C might be a property of the encoder rather than of proteins. On 13 August the same proteins were embedded with a second model and the whole subspace analysis re-run.

Design20,000 proteins, 5,000 from each of four domains, selected deterministically. The identical protein set is embedded twice, once with ESM-C 300M (960-d) and once with ESM-2 650M (1280-d), so the only variable is the encoder.
Dimension controlBoth reduced to the same 256 principal components before any analysis, so the two models share a dimension and the whitening is well conditioned at n/d of about 18.
Jobs47446873 (embedding, 20 minutes on one A100) and 47447997 (analysis)

One consistent difference between the models. ESM-2's raw subspace is slightly more load-bearing than ESM-C's (streptophyta 0.970 to 0.895 against 0.966 to 0.962). A caveat that applies only to the whitened columns. After whitening, the two subspaces occupy most of the available space (H is 69 to 185 of 256 dimensions), so the random-subspace null for their overlap rises to 0.49 to 0.84 and the measured overlap of 0.78 to 0.89 is barely above it. The containment result of the previous section is a raw-coordinate result, where the null is 0.20 to 0.55. In whitened coordinates the overlap statistic mostly reflects how large the subspaces are.

Does β mean what its name says in whitened units? The test, finally run

Since 6 August the document has carried an open item: β correlates positively with retained F1, which is the wrong sign for a damage measure, and the proposed explanation is that B is ordered by variance so "inside B" means "along a roomy axis". The proposed repair was to measure magnitude and β in whitened units. It had never been run. It has now.

DesignFor all 209 ordered group pairs, compute every geometry predictor twice: once in raw coordinates and once in coordinates whitened on the source domain only, which is the honest choice because at prediction time the target has not been seen. Correlate both against the same retention values from the 209-pair scan, with a group-level permutation null of 5,000 draws.

β: the repair works, but only conditionally, and it does not rescue the knob

The answer is a qualified yes. In raw coordinates β is robustly the wrong sign, and that is not a magnitude confound: the partial is +0.414 and it is positive in 14 of 15 source groups. Whitening flips the partial to −0.648, the correct sign for a damage measure, and it is negative in 11 of 15 groups. So the diagnosis was right.
But β still should not be used. Its marginal correlation in whitened units is −0.010, i.e. nothing, and it only becomes informative once magnitude is partialled out. Worse, whitened β has almost no spread left: a median of 0.017 with an interquartile range of 0.004 to 0.029. In whitened coordinates essentially none of the shift lands in the function subspace, so β is a near-constant quantity with the right sign and no dynamic range. The document's own standing criterion was "if β still does not go negative it should be dropped rather than defended". It goes negative only conditionally, and it is unusable either way. Drop it.

α: the knob that was written off is the one that works

α goes from ρ = −0.026 to ρ = −0.740 under whitening, and it holds within every one of the 15 source groups separately (median −0.807, range −0.916 to −0.192, 15 of 15 negative), so it is not a between-group artefact. Partialling out magnitude leaves −0.416.

Why it was invisible before: in raw coordinates the cosines between class displacement vectors are dominated by the few very high-variance directions, so every shift looks partly aligned and α is compressed into a narrow, uninformative band. Whitening gives every direction equal weight, and the cosine starts to mean what it is supposed to mean.

Read the sign carefully, because it is the opposite of the generator's assumption. Negative means higher α goes with lower retention: the more the classes move together, the more zero-shot damage. The generator assumes α = 1 (pure covariate shift) is the cheap regime. These are not in conflict, because they measure different things: retention is damage before adaptation, while r* is the cost of repairing it. A large shared translation badly displaces a fixed boundary and is also the easiest thing for a little target data to correct. Both can be true, and the document should stop treating α as a realism knob with no measurable consequence.
The honest limit. Whitened α and whitened magnitude are strongly collinear (ρ = +0.822), so roughly half of α's signal is shared with how far the shift went. The partial of −0.416 is what survives that, and the 15-of-15 within-group result is what rules out a group-level artefact.

What it showsv2's separation ratio of 1.10 sits just above the four ladder rungs at 1.00 and below Swiss-Prot to TrEMBL at 1.08 to 1.26. Its effective rank of 6.50 sits just below the ladder's 7.3, inside the real range of 6.2 to 10.7.

The knob spans 0 to 1 and can reproduce any of them, but there is no single real value to calibrate to, and the curation shift is far less shared than any taxonomic one.
Not in this figureIntrinsic dimension and Procrustes disparity, the two metrics that later proved the largest mismatches, are absent here. They are in the realism scorecard, which is why the scorecard changed the picture.

Why this matters nowβ was introduced to explain this panel and fitted to it. The fit reproduced four points. Measured on real data over 210 pairs, β has the opposite sign to the one this reasoning assumed. The panel is real and the phenomenon is real; what is not established is that β describes it. See the β evidence section.
CaveatThe real ladder has effectively two distinct distances, not four, so this is a weak test. It is reported as a consistency check, not as validation.

StatusThe chart holds. The claim that α therefore predicts adaptation cost does not survive real data: ρ(α damage) = +0.022, p = 0.87 over 210 real pairs. α is a realism knob, not a cost measure: §17.

Read across a row and you get the headline: at a fixed distance, lower α costs more labels. α = 1 is a rigid slide; the classes keep their arrangement, so the model needs relatively little help. α = 0 rearranges them, and the source model's boundary is genuinely wrong, so you need far more target data.

Read down a column and r* rises with distance until it becomes undefined; the budget can't reach the bar at any mix.

The ceiling column should be checked first in any of these tables. Across the whole α sweep the ceiling stays in the range 0.77–0.85: it barely moves. That flatness is the entire point of §11, and it's what makes these r* values comparable to each other at all.

Real side: gammaproteobacteria (64,791 proteins) against vertebrata (16,256), EC level 3, ESM-C. Synthetic side: v2 at d = 1.0, α = 0.59, β = 0.42, 12,000 samples per side, 125 classes. The src_gap and src_within_sigma ratios are omitted because the two sides are on different absolute scales; the scale-free comparison is the separation ratio.

The cautionary result from the same scorecard. Hubness originally measured 4.1× off and was on the must-fix list. With the synthetic class count matched to the real one (16 raised to 131) it is 0.98. The entire discrepancy was a class-count mismatch, and kNN label consistency shrank from 1.79 to 1.30 the same way. Match class counts before comparing anything synthetic to anything real.
The target matters too. Run against firmicutes instead of vertebrata, the real Procrustes disparity is 0.322 rather than 0.835 and real β is 0.807 rather than 0.404. The mismatch verdict does not change, but any single number quoted from this table should carry the target it was measured against.

Full historyThe six-stage history of this claim is on the Known objections page.

Zero-shot macro-F1 (upper block) and ceiling (lower block). Source: /scratch/lmk04992/synth_v2_beta_{0.05,0.15,0.30,0.50}/threshold_vs_distance.csv · job 47136848 · α = 1.0 throughout

Note the ceiling row. At d = 1.0 it reads 0.772, 0.774, 0.773, 0.773 across a tenfold change in β, while zero-shot falls from 0.705 to 0.399. β is a pure damage knob: it hurts the transferred model without making the task itself any harder. That is exactly the separation v1 could not achieve.
How this table was over-interpreted. β = 0.15 gives zero-shot 0.628, which sits right on the real eukaryote rungs (fungi 0.623, metazoa 0.640, plants 0.635), so β was “fitted” at 0.15 and described as the damage knob. Four points can be fit by many things. Measured on real data, β has the wrong sign in every operationalisation (ρ = +0.28 over 210 pairs), and under a matched control it is protective. See Q2.

Which generator knobs actually move r*

The distance, α and β knobs have been swept repeatedly. The structural knobs, the ones that define the universe rather than the shift, were calibrated once on 21 July and never varied. This sweep varies them one at a time from the calibrated configuration, holding d, α and β fixed, and asks how much of the r*(d) law is a property of the shift and how much is a property of the universe it happens in.

T7synthetic v2family labelsone knob varied at a timejob 47426352Which generator knobs actually move r*
What it isThe structure sweep: instead of moving the shift, this moves the universe, one generator knob at a time from the calibrated configuration, and asks how much of the r*(d) law belongs to the shift and how much to the world it happens in.
The findingr* is more sensitive to signal_dim than to the shift: 8→16 moves r* at d = 0.5 from 0.75 to 0.10, comparable to the entire calibrated distance range. The nuisance subspace, which is v2's central design achievement, moves r* by at most one grid step.
StatusHolds, and it undercuts the v2 design story. Listed among the open problems.

One knob at a time from the calibrated configuration. d ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}, α = 0.5, β = 0.5, mixing grid of 8, seeds 42/43/44. Job 47426352, 12 Aug 2026. /scratch/lmk04992/synth_v2_structure_cal/. r* at d = 1.0 is censored in every configuration except the two largest signal dimensions and is omitted for space.

The recovery threshold is more sensitive to the width of the signal subspace than to the shift. Moving signal_dim from 8 to 16, one knob, one step, moves r* at d = 0.5 from 0.75 to 0.10. For comparison, the entire calibrated distance range from d = 0.25 to d = 0.75 moves it from 0.20 to 1.00. The structural knob is doing work comparable to the thing being measured, and it was set once from an effective-rank match and never varied.
The nuisance subspace does not matter, which is worth saying out loud. Reproducing “gap approximately equals sigma yet F1 approximately 0.90” through a large power-law nuisance subspace was the central design achievement of v2. This sweep says that machinery has almost no influence on r*: 16 to 256 nuisance dimensions changes the ceiling by 0.02 and r* by at most one grid step. It buys realism in the geometry statistics and nothing in the measurement.

That is consistent with the subspace experiment on real data, where displacements outside both label subspaces were nearly harmless once coordinates were whitened.
Class count is a confound in every synthetic-to-real comparison in this document. Going from 16 to 32 classes raises r* at d = 0.25 from 0.20 to 0.75. The synthetic sweeps use 16 families; the real EC pairs have 30 to 112 classes. So the synthetic r* is systematically optimistic relative to a class-count-matched real comparison, by roughly the same margin as the distance effect being reported. This is landmine 2 of the brief, now quantified on the synthetic side rather than the real one.
A reproducibility trap found while setting this up, which matters for anyone rerunning the sweeps. The defaults compiled into src/run_distance_sweep_v2.py are not the calibrated values. Running the script without the full argument list silently gives a different universe:
Knobscript defaultcalibrated value, used in July

T8reproducibility noterun_distance_sweep_v2.pyA reproducibility trap in the sweep script
What it isNot a result. The defaults compiled into the sweep script are not the calibrated values, so running it without the full argument list silently produces a different universe.
Why it is hereAnyone rerunning these sweeps will get numbers that disagree with this page unless the calibrated arguments are passed explicitly.
The difference is not cosmetic: the defaults give a ceiling of 0.933 at d = 0 where the calibrated configuration gives 0.849, i.e. a materially easier task. The first version of this sweep was run on the defaults and discarded. The calibrated values are pinned explicitly in slurm/structure_sweep.slurm.
And one more instance of r* being fragile. The calibrated baseline here reproduces the July distance arm at every distance except d = 0.25, where it reports r* = 0.20 against July's 0.10. The only difference between the two runs is the list of distances requested, which changes the order in which random draws are consumed. Same configuration, same seeds, one grid step of disagreement.

The argument

Real data · homology labels

The July runs, all with Pfam labels: curation shift, the taxonomic ladder, and whether r* can be lowered

Before EC labels existed in this project, three separate real-data experiments were run: all of them predicting Pfam family, not function. They are the runs the synthetic generator was calibrated against, and they are where the “all real shifts are mild” finding comes from.

Every result on this page uses family labels. That was not a mistake; it was what the pipeline supported. But it means none of it answers the thesis question directly; it answers the homology version of it. The function version is the next page.

Building the real-data arm

Two environments, one A100, and one silent failure.

StepJobOutcome
Build the ESM-C conda environment46972331 EvolutionaryScale esm-3.2.1, separate env because it collides with fair-esm on import esm
GPU smoke test46972412 ESM-C 300M loads on an A100, returns shape (3, 960)
Embed Swiss-Prot → TrEMBL, both models46973912
46973913		 20,969 sequences embedded twice: identical sequences through ESM-C and ESM-2, which is what makes the comparison clean
Embed the taxonomy ladder46980032 Failed silently. pip install esm pulled torch 2.13+cu130; the GPU node it landed on had driver 12.8, so cuda.is_available() was False and it fell back to CPU: 30× slower. It ran 1 h 36 m and reached 5,700 of 36,981 before anyone noticed.
The fix. torch was repinned to 2.6.0+cu124 (runs on every A100 node the cluster has) and precompute_real_embeddings.py now fails loudly rather than crawling. The A100 nodes have mixed driver versions, so cu130 is a landmine, not a one-off.

Source: per-run *_batch_log.csv under /scratch/lmk04992/taxonomy_ladder/{archaea,fungi,metazoa,plants}/ · jobs 46980033–36 · r* recomputed as the smallest r reaching 0.9 × ceiling, 12 Aug 2026

Two observations, both used later. First, real taxa order sensibly by distance and bacteria→archaea (both prokaryotes) is much the closest, so there are really about two distinct real distances here, not four. Second, every real shift is mild: the worst degradation is 0.38, and 25% target data recovers even bacteria→plants. None of them reaches the synthetic curve’s knee, which sits at degradation above 0.9.
The r* definition problem was already visible here, in July. The recovery_summary.txt written by the job itself reports r* = 0.10 for all four targets, because it uses a return-to-baseline criterion. Recomputed against 0.9 × ceiling (the definition used everywhere else in this project) the same runs give 0.25 / 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.25.

And plants is decided by a hair: at r = 0.1 its final F1 is 0.7581 against a bar of 0.7599. It misses by 0.0018. Two defensible definitions, one dataset, different answers; a month before the same problem was rediscovered on EC labels and written up as the August headline.

Real embeddings: the ranking inverts

Zero-label adaptation, macro-F1, mean over seeds 42–44:

Shiftno adaptationCORAL OTBatchNormTENTceiling
swissprot → trembl0.8950.772 0.5520.8950.8940.945
bacteria → archaea0.7510.810 0.5740.8840.8870.943
bacteria → fungi0.6020.479 0.2970.6750.6760.873
bacteria → metazoa0.6260.542 0.3720.6710.6720.931
bacteria → plants0.6110.509 0.3940.6210.6260.806

Source: /scratch/lmk04992/threshold_lowering/real/real_results_table.md

Optimal transport is the best method on synthetic data and the worst on every single real shift, destroying 30 to 50 F1 points. That is not a bug and it was predicted before it was run. OT can undo a rotation perfectly when the class clusters are distinct, and collapses when they blur. Real Pfam clusters in ESM-C space have silhouette −0.02 to +0.04: they overlap almost completely, sitting at the far end of the synthetic identifiability ladder (which runs from 0.954 at σ = 0.5 down to 0.055 at σ = 6).

So the prediction was confirmed by correctly predicting a failure, which is a stronger test than confirming a success. It also refutes a premise the task inherited: Pfam families in embedding space are not distinct clusters.
The follow-up that separated two explanations. Was OT failing because it could not identify the shift, or merely because it could not estimate it from 1,000 samples in 960 dimensions? Job 47009884 swept unlabelled n from 250 to 6,000 on bacteria→{archaea, fungi}:

· CORAL improves with n (archaea 0.767 → 0.804, fungi 0.480 → 0.515), so estimation is real, but the gain is ~0.04 and never changes the ranking; on fungi CORAL never reaches the no-adaptation baseline at any n.
· OT is flat-broken at every n (~0.59 archaea, ~0.32 fungi): n-independent, so pure identifiability failure.
· BatchNorm is flat-best; it wins by capacity-matching (2×960 diagonal parameters, well determined from few samples), not by sample size.

Identifiability dominates; estimation is real but secondary.
Caveat, stated in the study’s own log. The agent that ran this found and fixed two of its own bugs mid-run, including a wrong-budget ceiling that made every method look identical; all pre-fix runs are invalid and were discarded. The synthetic and real arms were audited independently afterwards, and the numbers above are post-audit.

The argument

Real data · function labels

The August run: transfer measured against real EC labels on 231,285 proteins

Until August, every recovery threshold in this project (synthetic and real) was a Pfam (homology) threshold, while the thesis is about EC (function). This page is the run that finally measured r* against real EC labels, on 231,285 Swiss-Prot proteins across 15 taxonomic groups.

Summary. The robust quantity is not r*. It is zero-shot retention; what fraction of achievable performance a gammaproteobacterial model keeps with no target labels at all. It separates 8 bacterial targets (0.707–1.001) from 6 archaeal and eukaryotic ones (0.221–0.537) with nothing in between, in three configurations and two estimators. r* itself tells three different stories at three different budgets.

16 · The real-EC run

Until 7 August 2026, every recovery threshold in the project (synthetic and real) was a Pfam (homology) threshold. The thesis is about EC (function). The August run measured r* with EC labels on real proteins for the first time.

Setup: train on gammaproteobacteria (64,791 proteins: the biggest, best-studied group), test on 14 other taxonomic groups, predict EC level 3.

The finding that held

Define retention = zero-shot ÷ ceiling: how much of achievable performance you keep for free. It splits the tree of life cleanly:

Group typeretention
8 bacterial targets0.707 – 1.001
6 archaeal / eukaryotic targets0.221 – 0.537

A clean gap with nothing in it, 14 out of 14, across three configurations and two different model types. And the boundary falls between 36.7% and 42.0% sequence identity to the nearest training protein: straddling the ~40% threshold the enzyme literature independently gives for EC-level-3 annotation transfer. Nothing was tuned to land there.

The findings that didn't hold

  • r* itself is fragile. Same data, same model: at budget 200 it reads 0.0 for twelve of fourteen targets; at budget 1000 it cleanly reproduces the split; at 2000 it drifts again. Because the bar it's scored against is itself "a model trained on your P proteins", and that bar strengthens as P grows.
  • Six separate defects in the estimator were found and fixed: two of them inherited from the synthetic sweep's own code: adaptation running for only one pass, and a ceiling trained on 4× the pool. Which means the existing synthetic r*(d) curve is itself suspect and should be recomputed.
  • The generator is ~3× too optimistic about damage at the distance it was calibrated to. At d = 1.0 it predicts retention 0.10; the real gamma→plants comparison gives 0.29.

Two control arms, completed after the write-up

AUG7.md was written while the sweep was still running, and records arms 3 and 4 as “no output yet”. All four arms have since completed (/scratch/lmk04992/ec_rstar/ladder/rstar_{pair,matched,novelty,sizematched}.json). The two controls existed to ask whether the bacteria/non-bacteria split is an artifact rather than a finding. Neither says it is.

Control 1 · Class count

Arm _matched: the same 20 EC classes for every target: the ones shared by all 15 groups, core metabolism. Identical K-way problem everywhere, so K cannot explain anything. Budget 200, 3 seeds.

Target typeretention
8 bacterial0.817 – 1.007
6 archaeal / eukaryotic0.467 – 0.664

Clean gap again, 14 of 14: insecta 0.664, then nothing until actinobacteria 0.817. The split is not a class-count artifact.

Control 2 · Training-set size

Arm _sizematched: the source model is given exactly as many training proteins as the target has, removing gammaproteobacteria’s up-to-40× advantage. This is the arm directly comparable to the synthetic sweep, which draws equal n on both sides.

Target typeretention
8 bacterial0.583 – 0.942
6 archaeal / eukaryotic0.133 – 0.395

Still 14 of 14, gap from euryarchaeota 0.395 to bacteroidetes 0.583, but every number drops. Retention is partly bought with data volume; the ordering is not.

The key figure from the size-matched arm. Bacteroidetes falls from 1.001 to 0.583 once the source loses its data advantage. The headline “a big foreign training set beats a small native one outright” is true, and it is a statement about data volume as much as about biology. Both arms should be reported together; neither alone is honest.
And a caution the controls introduce. In the size-matched arm the absolute r* is nan (censored) for 22 of 28 rows, because a source model trained on as little as 930 proteins cannot reach 90% of a ceiling trained on the full reservoir at any mixing fraction. That is defect (d) of §3 in AUG7.md reappearing wherever the budget is small relative to the ceiling’s training set. Read the retention column, not the r* column.

The homology confound, quantified

A lookup table (family → most common EC, built from gammaproteobacteria, no model at all) scores 0.36 to 0.94 across the ladder. And what collapses with taxonomic distance is not the accuracy of the mapping (0.94 → 0.75) but the coverage (0.99 → 0.48): whether you've seen the family before.

But it isn't only homology. Restricted to a single Pfam family (so every protein is a relative of every other and homology is held constant) the model still separates EC classes at 0.95–1.00 and still transfers at 0.75–0.83, against a shuffled-label floor of 0.19–0.29. Real functional signal exists. (Caveat: only three families qualified.)

The new result. We built an axis nobody measures: hide a fraction of the EC classes from training entirely, so the model has never seen that chemistry. Hiding half the classes hurts about as much as jumping from bacteria to animals. The taxonomic axis (which the entire field measures) is the cheap one. The functional-novelty axis is where the cost actually is, and it's essentially unstudied.

EC transfers better than Pfam, in every direction tested

The same proteins, the same embeddings, the same probe: only the label changes. This is the comparison that motivated adding the EC axis at all, because it separates two claims that a family-conditioned measurement cannot: did the embedding move, or did it stop encoding function?

bacteria →EC zero-shotEC ceiling EC retainedPfam retaineddifference
archaea0.6540.9760.670 0.645+0.025
fungi0.5450.9640.565 0.473+0.092
metazoa0.5500.9910.556 0.549+0.007
plants0.7050.9770.721 0.688+0.033

Linear probe, 12 to 13 shared classes per label space, 2,077 to 3,046 target proteins. Source: /scratch/lmk04992/ec_analysis/ec_damage.json, job 47270164, 4 Aug 2026.

Taxonomic shift damages the homology readout more than the function readout. That is the opposite of the intuition that function is the fragile thing, and it is consistent in all four directions. It also means the two axes are genuinely different measurements rather than relabelled versions of each other.
And a strong asymmetry that a distance cannot express. Over all 20 ordered domain pairs, archaea → bacteria retains 0.508 while bacteria → archaea retains 0.670; plants → fungi retains 0.946 while fungi → plants retains 0.763. Direction of travel matters, and every symmetric distance metric in this project is blind to it.

Functional novelty, the constructed axis

Two different things get called distance, and only one of them has ever been measured. Moving to new organisms that perform the same chemistry is what the whole field measures. Encountering chemistry the training set never contained is essentially unstudied, because a natural version of the experiment does not exist in Swiss-Prot.

Why it had to be constructed. Gammaproteobacteria already contains nearly every EC class at level 3 that any other group has. Counting classes with at least 15 proteins in the target and zero in the source: nine of fourteen groups have none at all, and the largest case is 5 classes and 214 proteins. So the taxonomic ladder is close to pure covariate shift, and the novelty axis was built by deleting a fraction ν of EC classes from the source side of the problem.
F45real dataEC labels · level 3ec_swissprot · novelty arm · ESM-C 300Mjob 47292627Retention as chemistry is withheld
DatasetReal. 231,285 Swiss-Prot proteins, ESM-C 300M embeddings, source gammaproteobacteria (64,791 proteins), 14 target groups.
LabelsEC number, level 3. Not Pfam. Shared classes per pair, min 15 proteins each side.
DesignArm _novelty. A fraction ν of the shared EC classes is deleted from the source training data and from the source half of the pool, leaving them reachable only through the target half. The label space stays the union, so the model can still emit them. ν in {0, 0.25, 0.5}, budget 500, seeds 42/43/44.
What it showsAt ν = 0.5 the best bacterial target (spirochaetes, 0.373) is worse than most non-bacterial targets at ν = 0. Withholding half the chemistry from a near-identical bacterium costs about as much as crossing from bacteria to animals. The axis the field measures is the cheaper one.
Why constructed rather than foundChoosing a source group that lacks classes means choosing a small source group, which would confound novelty with training-set size. Deleting classes from the largest group avoids that.
LimitIt measures what happens when classes are withheld, not what happens in a real metagenome. Swiss-Prot does not contain the natural version of this experiment.

Which distance predicts the cost

Twenty-four candidate measures, each correlated against r* with a group-level permutation null (source held fixed, targets permuted, 5,000 draws). Grey bars did not reach significance.

The argument

Findings

What survived contact with real data, what did not, and why

A project’s corrections are more informative than its results. This page is everything that was confidently believed and turned out wrong, the three lessons underneath all of it, and the questions that are genuinely still open.

17 · Claims that did not survive

Recording overturned results explicitly is part of the method, not an admission against it.

"β is the damage knob: distance alone doesn't determine cost"
Overturned. On real data β has the wrong sign; higher β means less damage (ρ = +0.28). The earlier "β causally damages function" result came from an unfair control: the in-subspace direction was drawn from within the subspace, but the off-subspace direction was drawn isotropically across all 960 dimensions, which in high dimensions is nothing like any direction the data occupies. With both drawn fairly, β is protective. The likely explanation is that the signal subspace is by definition the high-variance directions, so a fixed-length step there is proportionally smaller. Unresolved. The proposed fix is to measure β in whitened units.
"α is related to the cost of adaptation"
Overturned. α predicts damage at ρ = +0.02, p = 0.87: literally nothing. It remains a good realism knob; it is not a cost measure. An independent re-run reproduced this (ρ = 0.086, p = 0.77).
"Scaffold change is unstructured"
Overturned by sample size. Came from 8 moves and 36 vectors on the small 16-family dataset. With 3,282 Pfam families it rests on 979 moves and gives the opposite answer. All three label axes turn out to be structured.
"Synthetic hubness is 4× off from real"
Evaporated. It was a class-count mismatch: 16 synthetic classes vs 131 real. Match the counts and the ratio is 0.98.
"The oracle generates the synthetic labels"
True in v0 only. Removed in v1 as a bug fix, because a globally consistent labeller makes negative transfer impossible. v1 and v2 label by family index.
"r* = 0.5 for non-bacterial targets"
Too strong. That was one estimator at one budget. r* moves between 0.0 and 0.75 for the same target depending on the budget. Retention is the stable quantity.
"The recovery threshold is ~0.5" (June, and reported in July)
Superseded at least three times. The real taxonomy ladder gave 0.10–0.25; curation shift gave ≈0.10; the EC ladder gives a budget-dependent number. The original rested on 3 seeds, a 5-point grid, one taxon pair, and a different definition of r*, with dip depths mostly inside the noise floor. The June note said so in its own caveats: the headline travelled and the caveat didn't.
"Optimal-transport feature alignment is the most robust way to lower the threshold"
Inverted on real data the same day it was found. Synthetically OT was best and could reach zero-label recovery. On real embeddings OT is the worst method on all five shifts (−0.21 to −0.34 F1) and simple batch-norm recalibration wins everywhere. Reason: real Pfam clusters in ESM-C space have silhouette 0.02–0.05, so there is no cluster structure for OT to transport. A rare case where a predicted failure confirmed the theory.
"Feature-Wasserstein distance is the x-axis"
Rejected. Non-monotone in d: it peaks at d = 0.5 and returns to ~0 at d = 1, because at d = 1 v1's target reused the same cluster locations with permuted labels. Wasserstein measures P(x) and is blind to label shift.
"The true α is 0.9–1.0; the measured 0.6 is inflated by centroid noise"
Backwards. Centroid noise is independent between classes, so it cancels in the numerator of a pairwise cosine while inflating both magnitudes: it biases α downward. Split-half reliability gives 0.97–0.99. Corrected α moves 0.594 → 0.611. α ≈ 0.6 stands.
"The dataset is what it is: 5 domains, 36,981 proteins"
It was an artifact of choosing 16 Pfam families. Swiss-Prot has 575,503 reviewed entries; 280,036 have an EC number; requiring a Pfam cross-reference costs only 0.8%. The 16 chosen families were the actual constraint. Rebuilt EC-first: 231,285 proteins, 15 groups, 210 pairs. A 6× data increase that had been available all along.

It runs the Aug-6 code on the old 5-domain data, which is what makes it a clean comparison: only n differs; n = 210 from ec_swissprot/analysis/beta_diagnosis.json (15 groups, 117 EC classes, subspace dim 22, job 47289440).

Four of twelve predictors change sign. Not magnitude, sign. At n = 20 a group-level permutation test over 5 domains has only 120 possible arrangements, so nothing could reach significance regardless of whether it was true. Two predictors did cross p < 0.05 there, which is roughly what twelve tests produce by chance. Any conclusion drawn from the left-hand columns was a coin flip with a decimal point on it.

17b · Three recurring failure modes

1. Every wrong answer came from a bar that moved

v1's ceiling moved with distance. The adaptation-method study had a mis-budgeted ceiling. Last week's full-reservoir ceiling moved with the target's data volume. And the fix for that introduced a budget ceiling that moves with the budget. Four times. The rule "always report the ceiling next to r*" was written after the first three and violated immediately afterwards.

2. Controls and denominators decide conclusions more often than data does

β flips sign between an isotropic control and a matched one. "Scaffold change is unstructured" flipped because a within-move statistic was compared against a cross-move one. The 4× hubness discrepancy was entirely a class-count mismatch. In every one of those cases the measurement was fine: the comparison wasn't.

3. The evidence for a bug is usually already in your logs

The U-shaped ceiling was measured on 14 July and explained away; it was believed on 22 July. A GPU smoke test "passed" on the one node in a heterogeneous pool where it could, hiding a silent CPU fallback that cost a 30× slowdown. In both cases nothing new was measured: someone just looked again.

18 · Open questions

  1. Recompute the synthetic r*(d) curve with the repaired estimator. Two of the six defects found on 7 August live in the synthetic sweep's own code. Its "never recovers" points above d=0.75 may be artifacts. This is cheap and should be done first.
  2. Whitened β. The one change that could make β mean what its name says. Contained.
  3. The functional-novelty axis. Newest, least studied, largest effect. Best claim to novelty.
  4. Run BLAST for all 210 group pairs. Turns the sequence-identity result from 14 points into 210 and makes it publishable rather than suggestive.
  5. Repeat one arm with a different embedding model (ESM-2). ESM-C is the best taxonomy detector of any protein language model tested, so we may be measuring the model's taxonomic sensitivity rather than biology. This would settle it.
  6. Heavy-tailed within-family oracle labels, if the EC-like synthetic label space is still wanted.

Where the subspace result sits in the literature

A literature check was run on 13 August specifically to find out which parts of the subspace finding are new. The answer is uncomfortable in a useful way: the mechanism is well established outside biology, and what is new is the measurement in this domain.

Our findingStatusWhy
Function subspace sits inside homology subspace, 85 to 92% of EC variance, principal angles 0.84 to 0.97 against nulls of 0.20 to 0.55, in two encoders novel as a measurement No paper computes principal angles between homology-defined and function-defined subspaces of protein embeddings. The phenomenon, that evolutionary signal dominates and confounds function prediction, is published.
Raw deletion harmless, whitened deletion catastrophic not novel as a principle Anticipated in 1983 for discriminant analysis, demonstrated for transformer embeddings in 2021, and formalised by concept-erasure theory in 2023, whose erasure operator whitens, projects and unwhitens. Our conclusion is their design decision, arrived at empirically.
Out-of-subspace displacement damaging when raw, harmless when whitened weakest; partly a units artefact A fixed Euclidean displacement is an enormous perturbation in units of within-class spread along a narrow direction and a small one along a wide direction, so part of the contrast restates the change of metric. Measured directly: at two gaps in raw coordinates the same nominal displacement is 8 to 10 within-class standard deviations inside B but 17 to 29 outside it.
The correction that matters most. Concept-erasure theory says a classification task is linearly guarded if and only if every class has the same mean, which requires zeroing the entire column space of the representation-label covariance. We removed a 90%-variance truncation of it. Those two facts are consistent, and the gap between them is the whole content of our result: the residual 10% of raw between-class variance carries essentially all of the discriminability, because those directions have small within-class variance. Under whitening, variance rank and discriminative rank coincide, which is the classical PCA-against-LDA distinction.
How to claim it. Not as "we discovered that top principal components are not the discriminative ones", which has been known since 1983. The defensible claim is narrower and still worth making: the raw-coordinate low-rank centroid subspace, which is the natural thing to build and is what a published attribute-removal method builds, retains essentially none of the EC-discriminative signal in protein embeddings, while the whitened subspace at the same rank retains nearly all of it, in four taxonomic domains and two encoders. That is a validated methodological warning for protein-embedding interpretability.
One published result cuts against us and should be cited rather than avoided. A 2025 study using cross-species complementation as a functional gold standard reports ESM-C embeddings outperforming a sequence-identity baseline, 21 of 22 against 19 of 22. That is the strongest published argument that these embeddings carry function beyond homology. It rests on 22 triplets and a two-protein margin, which is the honest basis on which to weigh it, but a reader who knows the field will raise it.
The nearest prior work on the protein side tests whether embeddings can decide if two proteins share a species, and finds most models exceed 0.8 F1, concluding that networks exploit phylogenetic distance rather than genuine functional features. It covers ESM-C 300M and 600M directly. Our design differs in a way worth stating: we work entirely within one taxonomic group at a time, so taxonomy is held constant and what remains is the homology-against-function cut.

The argument

Known objections

The standing challenges to this work, and the current answer to each

The objections this work has to answer, each with the current answer and its weakest point. The first group is short; the second group is examined in full, because those five go to the heart of the method. β is the item that moved most: it reversed sign twice.

Standing objections, in brief

Does the synthetic data actually resemble reality?
Seven geometric quantities were measured on real embeddings and used to set the knobs (§14), and the resulting synthetic data was checked against held-out real behaviour. Honest answer: it matches on geometry, and it is about 3× too pessimistic on transfer damage at the distance it was calibrated to. That gap is unexplained.
Is the model just doing homology lookup?
Partly, and we measured it rather than guessing: a family→EC lookup with no model gets 0.36–0.94. But within a single family, where homology is constant, the model still works far above a shuffled-label floor. So: substantially homology, not only homology. Weakest link is that only three families qualified for that control.
"Why EC level 3 and not level 4?"
Level 4 is the exact reaction and largely encodes substrate specificity; level 3 is the chemistry. The literature threshold for reliable transfer is ~40% sequence identity at level 3 versus ~60% at level 4, and published benchmarks find most level-4 errors are correct through level 3. It's the defensible level, and we can say why.
What is r* actually good for?
Telling a scientist their annotation budget before they label anything, from quantities they can compute in advance: sequence identity to their nearest known protein, or which branch of the tree they've sampled. That's the practical payoff, and the August result gives a usable rule: above ~42% identity you need essentially nothing; below ~37% you need a third to a half of your budget to be native.
Has anyone done this before?
r* is the empirical instantiation of Ben-David et al. (2010), who derive an optimal source/target mixing weight with a phase transition at an absolute target sample count: it is cited directly. What appears genuinely unoccupied: no mainline EC predictor splits by taxonomy, and nobody has mapped a label-free distance measure onto a labelling budget in proteins.
Why does the synthetic side label by family when the thesis is about function?
This is the strongest open objection. Answer: because removing the oracle in v1 was necessary to make negative transfer possible at all, and family index was the simplest consistent label. The August work tried to build an EC-like label space on top and hit a purity/coverage conflict that isn't solved. So the synthetic arm currently simulates homology recovery; the real arm now measures function recovery directly. Closing that is open work.

Five objections, examined in full

Five objections that go to the heart of the method, each stated in full, answered, and followed by what has changed since it was first raised. Several of these answers have since changed, β most of all.

Where each one stands: Q1 stands unchanged. Q2's answer reversed sign twice and is still unresolved. Q3 was correct and has been fixed; the dataset is now 6× bigger. Q4's premise turned out to be an artifact, and the conclusion is the opposite of what it looked like. Q5 has a concrete answer plus one item added in August.

Q1 · What exactly is the "typical distance"?

"on the magnitude of the vector, it divides |v|/gap, where gap is the 'typical distance between two EC groups'. What is this 'typical distance'? The average distance between EC groups if you compute all pairwise distances? Or something else?"

It is the all-pairs average. Precisely:

gap = mean over ALL pairwise Euclidean distances between EC-group centroids, computed in the source domain only, over EC groups with ≥ min_n proteins there

Three details that matter and are easy to miss:

  • Centroids, not proteins. Each EC group is collapsed to its average position first. The distance between two individual proteins is much larger: 1.57× the gap.
  • Source domain only. Computed inside gammaproteobacteria alone, so the ruler is independent of the shift being measured against it.
  • All pairs, unweighted mean. On the current dataset: 131 centroids → 8,515 pairwise distances. (On the old 16-family set it was 18 → 153.)

Because "typical" could reasonably mean several things, all the alternatives were computed. As multiples of the gap actually used:

Alternative definition× the gap in use
median pairwise centroid distance0.95
10th-percentile pairwise distance0.58
closest pair of centroids0.24
pooled over all taxonomic groups (not just source)1.09
Pfam centroids instead of EC centroids1.29
two random individual proteins1.57
The number to quote alongside every |v|/gap. The separation ratio gap ÷ within-EC σ = 1.11. EC groups sit about one within-group width apart. So "|v|/gap = 1.2" means the shift is slightly larger than the spacing between functional classes, and that spacing is itself about the size of one class. That context changes how big the number feels.

Status. No. Definition unchanged; only the sample grew (18 → 131 centroids).

Q2 · How can β be positive if B is defined as the function dimensions?

"on the 'b does not predict damage' section, you show the correlation between b of the shared translation vs zero-shot F1 and it's positive rather than negative as you'd expect. I don't understand how that would be if you explicitly define B as the dimensions which differentiate function? Wouldn't this by definition result in lower B (more function damaging) the closer to 1 the B parameter is? How were those functionally-relevant dimensions of ESM-C determined in this experiment?"

The reasoning is exactly right, and the result still contradicts it. That contradiction is unresolved. Taking the two parts separately.

How B was determined

1. take every EC group's centroid, in the source domain only 2. mean-centre them 3. SVD → the directions along which EC centroids differ most 4. keep the top k holding 90% of the between-EC variance → k = 22 of 960 on the current data (8 on the old 16-family set)

Fitted on the source domain only, so B is independent of the shift later projected onto it. β = the fraction of the shift's squared length lying inside B.

Why the expectation fails: B is chosen for spread, and length is measured in raw units

Step 4 selects the directions where centroids are most spread out, by construction, the high-variance directions. But the shift is measured in plain Euclidean length. So "one unit of movement" is not comparable across directions:

along a wide signal direction, classes sit ~10 units apart → moving 1 unit barely changes which class you resemble along a narrow direction, classes sit ~0.5 units apart → moving 1 unit throws you past two classes

β is confounded with how wide the direction travelled is. It looks protective because "inside B" mostly means "along a wide axis", not because signal directions are safe.

See it: same distance, opposite outcome

Four classes. They are separated a lot left-to-right (the wide direction; this is the one SVD picks first, so it is what goes into B) and only a little up-and-down (the narrow direction). Now shift everything by a fixed distance and rotate which way it points. The arrow never changes length.

F48in-browser illustrationEC labels · level 3drawn from gammaproteobacteria · ESM-C 300Mjob 47289440Same distance, opposite outcome: why β misbehaves
What it isAn illustration: four classes separated a lot along a wide direction and a little along a narrow one, with a fixed-length shift you rotate.
DatasetNone: drawn live. But the geometry it dramatises is measured.
The measured fact behind itOn real gammaproteobacteria (167 EC centroids, B = top 22 of 960 by SVD), centroid spread along the directions of B runs 0.176 / 0.078 / 0.039 / 0.016; the widest is 11.3× the narrowest. In the generator that ratio is exactly 1.0.
Where that came fromjob 47289440 · src/measure_ec_geometry.py, src/beta_diagnosis.py · /scratch/lmk04992/ec_swissprot/analysis/ · 6 Aug 2026. Real ESM-C, EC level-3 labels.
ProvenanceIllustration built to explain a real measurement. Do not quote numbers off the canvas; quote the 11.3× ratio and the four spreads.
Relatedjob 47289440: the EC geometry battery · the full answer on β
Work through it in order.

1. Leave the direction at 0°. The shift runs entirely along the wide direction, so it is entirely inside B, i.e. β = 1. Accuracy barely moves. The classes are 6 units apart along this axis; sliding them 0.6 is nothing.

2. Now drag the direction to 90°. Same arrow length. Now the shift is entirely along the narrow direction: entirely outside B, i.e. β = 0. Watch the accuracy collapse. The classes are only 0.68 apart here, so sliding 0.6 nearly swaps them.

Identical Euclidean distance. β = 1 is harmless; β = 0 is catastrophic. Therefore high β correlates with LESS damage: exactly the "+0.28" that looked impossible.

And notice what did not happen: at no point did the wide direction stop being "function-relevant". It separates classes perfectly well: it's the direction that separates them most. It is simply so roomy that a fixed-size step doesn't matter there. β ranks moves by elbow room, and the fact that B was chosen for "where classes differ most" never enters the causal story at all.

Supporting evidence from the real data: off-subspace displacement predicts damage nearly twice as strongly (ρ = −0.595) as in-subspace displacement (ρ = −0.367); exactly what the demo above predicts.

And there was a second, separate error: a control that wasn't matched. The earlier claim "β causally damages function" came from an injection experiment where the in-subspace direction was drawn from within B, but the off-subspace direction was drawn isotropically across all 960 dimensions. In high dimensions a uniformly random direction resembles nothing the data occupies. So the contrast wasn't "in B vs out of B"; it was "a realistic direction vs a bizarre one".
controlin-B drawn fromoff-B drawn fromverdict
isotropicuniform in Buniform in ℝ⁹⁶⁰β damages
on-manifolduniform in Bdata covarianceno clear effect
matcheddata covariancedata covarianceβ protects
Under the matched control, retained F1 rises monotonically with β: 0.116 → 0.489 at 2 gaps, 0.520 → 0.923 at 1 gap.
How the β claim changed, in order.
WhenClaim about βStatus
July 22β is the damage knob; fitted at β ≈ 0.15retracted
Aug 4measured directly in EC space: β = 0.42, not 0.15value changed
Aug 4β has the wrong sign (+0.32 / +0.38) vs retained F1stands
Aug 4injection says β causally damages functionwrong: unmatched control
Aug 6matched control: β is protective, monotonically. Real data +0.280, p = 0.006stands
Aug 7reproduced independently at +0.297; against r*, ρ = −0.288, p = 0.33stands
So β changed value (0.15 → 0.42), changed sign of effect (damaging → protective), and had a causal claim retracted. The current position: β is not a damage knob and should not be described as one.
The proposed fix, not yet run. Define both β and magnitude in whitened units; rescale each direction by how much the source data actually varies along it, so "one unit" means the same thing everywhere. Then re-test whether β goes negative as its name implies. It is a contained change to measure_ec_geometry.py and has been on the list since Aug 6. If it still doesn't go negative, β should be dropped rather than defended.

Q3 · Why only 20–30k proteins?

"also surprised we only have 20-30k proteins - did we subset on something? Maybe because we're requiring Pfam numbers? I think there's 200k-300k-ish of Swissprot proteins with EC numbers."

Correct that it was subset, and the 200–300k figure is right: 280,036. The diagnosis of why was wrong, and the real cause was worse.

Queryproteins
Swiss-Prot reviewed575,503
… with an EC number280,036← the published figure
… and a Pfam cross-reference277,716← requiring Pfam costs only 0.8%
… and in our 16 chosen families36,981← the actual constraint
… and a single unambiguous EC at level 320,285

Requiring Pfam was almost free. The bottleneck was that the dataset had been built family-first around 16 hand-picked Pfam families; a decision inherited from a much earlier stage of the project and never revisited. It threw away 87% of the usable proteins.

Fixed. The dataset was rebuilt EC-first rather than family-first:
20,285 → 231,285 proteins (11× more) 5 → 15 usable taxonomic groups 102 → 270 EC groups 16 → 3,282 Pfam families
Groups are now assigned at phylum/class level from the NCBI lineage, so euryarchaeota and crenarchaeota are separate and the five proteobacterial classes are separate.

Why this mattered more than the raw count. 5 groups gave 20 ordered pairs, and a group-level permutation test over 5 groups has only 120 possible arrangements: nothing could reach significance no matter what was true. 15 groups give 210 pairs, and 9 of the 12 damage predictors became significant. Two AUG4 conclusions fell immediately as a result. This single fix retroactively rescued or killed most of the earlier analysis.

Status. Entirely. This is the fix that made everything else possible.

Q4 · Is α ≈ 0 for functional shifts?

"I also feel like we are still over-measuring the domain shift and under-measuring the Pfam or EC shift; it looks like we have consistent Alpha when we're looking at how we move from bacteria->plants or other domain shifts, but we have alpha much closer to 0 when we look at EC shifts (hold domain constant, of Pfam constant, or both, and see how we shift from EC1 to EC2) - am I reading that right?"
No, and this is the most consequential correction of the five. The numbers being compared were not the same statistic, and the one that looked like α ≈ 0 rested on 8 moves and 36 vectors.

The error. The taxonomic α (+0.59) was a within-move number: fix one move (bacteria→plants) and ask whether it looks the same across different contexts. The functional α (+0.08) was a cross-move number: pool cosines across different EC→EC pairs. Different moves point in different directions, so of course that averages toward zero. It would do so even if functional shift were perfectly structured.

See the error, and the fix

Each panel is a bundle of shift vectors, drawn from the centre. Tightly bundled = high α (they all point the same way). Scattered = α ≈ 0. Press the two buttons to see which panels were compared, versus which should have been.

The measurements it drawsEC|DOM: within +0.531, cross +0.008, over 4,000 distinct EC→EC moves and 50,400 cosines. TAX|EC: within +0.696, cross +0.054, 105 moves. All eight conditioned shifts have their own cross-move null.
Where that came fromjob 47289440 · src/ec_permutations.py · /scratch/lmk04992/ec_swissprot/analysis/ · 6 Aug 2026
StatusThe correction holds: functional shift is strongly structured (excess +0.523), and the earlier “α ≈ 0 for functional shifts” came from comparing a within-move number against a cross-move one on 8 moves. §20 Q4.
Relatedjob 47289440: the permutation battery · the full answer on α
What the four panels are.
within = take one move (say "EC 1.1.1 → 2.7.1"), and measure it separately in many different taxonomic groups. Do those arrows agree? If the move means the same thing everywhere, they bundle tightly.
cross = take different moves (1.1.1→2.7.1, then 3.1.1→4.2.1, then others), and compare those. Different moves genuinely go different places, so these scatter no matter how structured the data is.

Cross-move is a baseline, not a measurement. It tells you what "no structure" looks like for that shift type. The only meaningful quantity is how far above its own baseline a within-move number sits, which is why the column that matters is excess = within − cross.

The fix. Compute all 8 conditioned shift types, each with its own cross-move null, on the rebuilt dataset. The meaningful quantity is excess = within − cross.

How to read the notation in the table. The bar means "holding fixed". TAX|EC = move across taxonomy while holding EC constant (same enzyme, different organism). EC|DOM = move from one EC to another while holding the taxonomic domain constant (same organism group, different chemistry). FAM|EC,DOM = change Pfam family while holding both EC and domain fixed (same chemistry, same organisms, different ancestry).

within = fix one move and see whether it looks the same across contexts. cross = pool across different moves, which averages toward zero even under perfect structure. excess = within − cross is the honest measure, because it subtracts that baseline off.
