Functional shift is strongly structured. EC|DOM gives an excess of +0.523 over 4,000 distinct EC→EC moves and 50,400 cosines. Moving from EC e₁ to EC e₂ produces close to the same displacement vector in every taxonomic group, which is exactly the generator's structural assumption.

And it is not an artifact of coarse binning: at EC level 4 (the exact reaction) the excess is higher, +0.635.

All three label axes are structured, with excesses of +0.52 to +0.64 against cross-move nulls of ≈ 0. The two rows that look unstructured are the two with 24 and 21 vectors.

You also asked for more permutations to be reported. All eight are now computed and are in the table above; that request was implemented directly.

A deeper concern stands, and it is the sharpest objection available. The question is whether the synthetic data emulates functional shift as well as taxonomic shift. The honest answer is we still don't know, because:
  • the synthetic generator labels its proteins by family, not by EC, so the synthetic side has been simulating homology recovery all along;
  • the attempt to give it an EC-like label space hit an unresolved purity/coverage conflict (§13);
  • the real EC measurements now exist (they're §16), but the synthetic side has not been re-fitted against them.
Closing that is genuinely open work.

Status. Yes; the premise was overturned. What looked like "functional shift is unstructured" was an artifact of comparing two different statistics on 8 moves.

Q5 · Should we measure anything beyond magnitude, α and β?

"and just flagging here that we should brainstorm whether we should be measuring anything else in addition to magnitude, alpha, and beta to measure how well our synthetic embedding space tracks with real world embeddings, or if our current metrics are sufficient"

Yes; the current three are demonstrably insufficient, and there is now a ranked answer. A full scorecard was run comparing v2 at its calibrated settings against real embeddings, with class count matched (which matters: see the footnote).

First: what each of these metrics actually measures

Eleven statistics get quoted below and none of them is self-explanatory. Each one is a different way of asking "does the fake data look like the real data?", and they catch different failures.

Hubness

Do a few points hog all the "nearest neighbour" slots? Take everyone's 10 nearest neighbours. Now count how often each point appears in someone else's list. In a fair world everyone appears about 10 times. In high dimensions they don't: a handful of points become hubs, showing up in hundreds of lists, while others appear in none.

Measured as the skew of that count. Real embeddings are hub-heavy; plain round-blob mixtures are not, so this separates them sharply.

Why care: anything that works by neighbourhoods (kNN classifiers, retrieval, clustering) behaves differently in a hub-heavy space. Ratio 0.98: matches essentially perfectly.

kNN label consistency

Of your 10 nearest neighbours, how many share your label? That's it. A direct measure of how cleanly the space clusters by label.

Why care: a synthetic space can match every centroid statistic and still get this wrong, and this is what a classifier trained on a small sample actually feels. Ratio 1.30; synthetic is ~30% too tidy locally.

Additivity

Do two labels' effects simply add up? Take the grid of (Pfam × EC) combinations. Each cell has a position. Ask: is cell (family f, enzyme e) predictable as [where family f sits] + [what enzyme e does]? If yes → additive. Whatever can't be predicted that way is interaction.

Pfam × EC grid: 99.4% additive (0.6% interaction) group × EC grid: 78.7% additive (21% interaction)

Why care; this one is load-bearing. The generator assumes additivity: it builds a target position as source position + a shift. If real biology were strongly interactive, that whole structure would be wrong. It's ~79–99% right, so the assumption holds broadly and misses about a fifth on the taxonomy axis. Ratio 0.90.

Shared fraction

How much of the movement is the flock, versus the wobble? (§8.) The share of the shift that is common to every class. Closely related to α, with exactly two groups, interaction share is literally 1 − shared fraction. Ratio 0.92.

Effective rank

How many directions does the cloud really use? Nominally 960. But if the data is nearly flat along most of them, the honest answer is far smaller. Computed as a "participation ratio" of the variance spectrum: a smooth count that ignores the long tail of near-zero directions.

Real embeddings: 3–11 of 960. Ratio 1.34.

Intrinsic dimension : 8.6× off

How many dimensions does the data occupy locally? Different question from effective rank, which is global. Estimated from the ratio of the distance to your 1st versus 2nd nearest neighbour; if points sit on a thin curve those two distances are similar; if they fill a fat blob they differ.

real: 1.77 v2: 15.17 v2 is too FULL locally dims to 90% variance: real: 55 v2: 12 v2 is too COMPACT globally

Reading: real proteins sit on thin filaments spread through a large space. v2 produces fat blobs packed into a small one. Both numbers are wrong, in opposite directions, which is why both are reported.

Class-covariance heterogeneity : 3.2× off

Do different classes have differently-shaped clouds? Not different sizes: different shapes. Take each class's cloud, find the direction it's most stretched along, and ask whether two classes are stretched the same way. Averaged over all pairs.

real: 0.284 classes point in genuinely different directions v2: 0.920 every class is nearly the same shape

Why: the generator gives every family the same covariance, merely rescaled, so all classes are stretched identically and this pins near 1. Real families are shaped differently from one another. Cheap fix: give each class its own random rotation of the covariance.

Procrustes disparity : 12× off · the important one

How much does the constellation of classes genuinely rearrange? Take the class centroids before and after the shift. Slide, spin and resize one to match the other as well as you possibly can. Whatever mismatch is left over is the Procrustes disparity.

So it deliberately ignores translation, rotation and scale, and measures only the residue: did the shape actually change? Zero = same constellation, just moved. Large = genuinely reshuffled.

real: 0.322 real shifts genuinely deform the arrangement v2: 0.026 v2 barely deforms it at all
And the reason is structural, not a tuning miss. v2's family-specific motion is a rotation; chosen deliberately in §11 because rotations are isometries and keep the ceiling flat. But a rotation by definition preserves the shape of the constellation, so its Procrustes disparity is near zero by construction. The very choice that fixed the moving-ceiling bug is what makes this metric impossible to match.

Negative-transfer dip depth : added August 2026

How far below its own starting point does the model fall during adaptation, before recovering? (§4.) Real: 0.10–0.30 for every group. Synthetic: its largest dips occur at d = 0, where nothing has moved, so they are the noise floor.

The remaining two: α and |v|/gap; are §8 and §20 Q1 respectively.

Metricrealv2Why it's first

Item 1 is the most important of the four. Procrustes disparity measures how much the configuration of classes rearranges, independent of translation and scale. It is 12× off, and it predicts damage better than |v|/gap does. That combination (badly mismatched and strongly predictive) is exactly the profile of a missing knob. α, β and magnitude cannot express it at all, because the generator's family-specific term is a rigid rotation, which by construction has near-zero Procrustes disparity.
A cautionary result from the same scorecard, worth repeating. Hubness originally looked 4.1× off and was on the "must fix" list. With the synthetic class count matched to the real one (16 → 131 classes) it is 0.98. The entire discrepancy was a class-count mismatch. kNN consistency shrank 1.79 → 1.30 the same way. Match class counts before comparing anything synthetic to anything real, or you will chase artifacts.

Status. Extended; three metrics were identified then, and a fourth (dip depth) was added in August.

The record

Lab ledger

Dated entries: what was run, the command, and where the output lives

A dated log of what was run, by whom or by what, with the exact command and the exact output path. Newest first. Anything in this document that carries a number should be traceable from here to a file on /scratch and a command that regenerates it.

How to read an entry. Every entry states the question, the command, the output location, and the verdict. Where an entry changed something elsewhere in this document, it says which page. Where it found nothing, it says that too, because a null check is still a check.

12 August, evening · New experiment: is the signal/nuisance split real?

Where the question came from. A question logged on 12 August asked how the signal and nuisance dimensions would differ depending on the protein language model and the label axis, and specifically: if data is shifted along the homology subspace, what does that do to function prediction? That is a question the generator cannot answer, because in the generator the signal subspace is declared rather than discovered, and there is only one label axis. On real embeddings there are two.

H = the directions along which Pfam families separate homology B = the directions along which EC classes separate function

If H and B were orthogonal, homology and function would be independently readable, and a shift along H would leave function prediction untouched. If B sits inside H, then an EC probe is largely reading homology and any homology-directed shift damages it.

Command, exactly as run.

sbatch slurm/subspace.slurm # job 47425149, raw units sbatch slurm/subspace2.slurm # job 47425234, adds random controls and whitened units python src/subspace_experiment.py --outdir /scratch/lmk04992/subspace \ --domain gammaproteobacteria --max_n 20000 --min_n_ec 30 --min_n_fam 30 \ --seeds 42 43 44 --mags 0.5 1.0 2.0

Inputs: the existing ESM-C cache ec_swissprot/emb_cache_esmc.npy, unchanged. Nothing was re-embedded. Output: /scratch/lmk04992/subspace{,2}/subspace_<domain>{,_whitened}.json. Script committed at src/subspace_experiment.py.

Result, in one line. Between 83% and 91% of the EC between-class variance lies inside the Pfam subspace, in all four domains tested, and in raw coordinates deleting either subspace costs nothing while in whitened coordinates deleting either one is catastrophic. Full write-up on the generator design page.
JobIDWhatOutput
subspace47425149 4 domains, raw coordinates/scratch/lmk04992/subspace/
subspace247425234 4 domains, raw and whitened, plus random matched-dimension controls /scratch/lmk04992/subspace2/

13 August · Two-model replication, and the whitened repair

Questions. Two were left open on 12 August. Is the homology/function entanglement a property of ESM-C or of proteins? And does measuring β in whitened units rescue it?

Commands.

sbatch slurm/whitened_geometry.slurm # 47446872 sbatch slurm/esm2_ec_embed.slurm # 47446873, one A100, 20 min sbatch slurm/subspace_plm2.slurm # 47447997, the corrected comparison
Results. Both subspace findings replicate under ESM-2, so they are not encoder artefacts (write-up). The whitening repair works for β only conditionally and leaves it unusable, while α, previously written off, becomes a strong predictor (write-up).
Discarded run, recorded. Job 47447417 was the first two-model comparison and is invalid: applying a min_n of 30 to a 5,000-protein subsample left 463 proteins for gammaproteobacteria against 960 dimensions, and whitening below n = d spheres the sample exactly. The symptom was that the whitened rows came out identical for two different models. Corrected by scaling min_n and projecting both encoders to a common 256 principal components.
A referee objection closed. A fixed Euclidean displacement is not a fixed intervention: measured directly, two gaps in raw coordinates is 8 to 10 within-class standard deviations inside the function subspace but 17 to 29 outside it. The displacement result is therefore partly a statement about units, and is now reported as the weakest of the three findings. See the positioning section.

12 August, evening · New experiment: which generator knobs move r*

Question. d, α and β have been swept repeatedly. The structural knobs were calibrated once on 21 July and never varied. How much of the r*(d) law is a property of the shift, and how much of the universe it happens in?

Command.

sbatch slurm/structure_sweep.slurm # job 47426352 # one knob at a time from the calibrated configuration, which must be pinned # explicitly because the script defaults are NOT the calibrated values python src/run_distance_sweep_v2.py --outdir /scratch/lmk04992/synth_v2_structure_cal/<tag> \ --distances 0.0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0 --alphas 0.5 --beta 0.5 --seeds 42,43,44 \ --signal_dim 8 --nuisance_dim 64 --centroid_spread 3.0 --sigma_signal 1.5 \ --nuisance_ratio 3.0 --spectrum_exponent 2.0 --family_sigma_spread 1.9 \ --family_size_skew 36.0 --d_unit_gaps 1.2 --ambient_sigma 0.0 \ --target_sigma_inflate 0.15 --n_families 16 --universe_seed 7 <override>
Result, in one line. signal_dim moves r* more than the shift does; the entire nuisance subspace moves it almost not at all; class count moves it a lot. Full write-up on the v2 results page.
Discarded run, recorded so it is not mistaken for a result. The first version of this sweep (job 47425259, /scratch/lmk04992/synth_v2_structure/) used the script defaults rather than the calibrated values and therefore ran around the wrong centre point: ceiling 0.933 at d = 0 rather than 0.849. Its 12 output directories are kept but should not be quoted. The corrected sweep is 47426352 in synth_v2_structure_cal/.

12 August, evening · Independent re-derivation of every synthetic number

Question. The v1 and v2 sweeps each write two files: the raw per-run sweep_results.csv, and the pipeline's own aggregated threshold_vs_distance.csv. Every number quoted in this document comes from the second file. Does the second file follow from the first, under the r* definition this project claims to use?

r* = the smallest mixing fraction r on the grid at which the mean over seeds of the final target macro-F1 reaches 0.9 × ceiling. undefined if no r on the grid reaches it

Method. Recompute ceiling, zero-shot, the mean final-F1 curve and r* from sweep_results.csv alone, for all ten sweep directories, and compare cell by cell. Then read the two sweep drivers to confirm what they actually do rather than what the notes say.

CheckedCellsVerdict
ceiling per (distance, alpha)76 76 / 76 agree
r* per (distance, alpha)76 76 / 76 agree
mean final-F1 curvesall agree to 6.7e-05, i.e. display rounding
dip depths, v2 distance arm16 agree to 5e-04, i.e. rounding of the seed mean

Directories: synth_distance_sweep, _hardceil, _sigma4.0, _sigma6.0, synth_v2_distance, _alpha_sweep, _beta_{0.05,0.15,0.30,0.50}. Drivers read: src/run_distance_sweep.py lines 203–206 and src/run_distance_sweep_v2.py lines 178–183.

The specific worry that prompted this, and its answer

There are two ways to turn per-seed curves into one threshold, and they are not the same number: take the threshold of the seed-mean curve, or take the mean of the per-seed thresholds. The second is a common and silent error.

The pipeline does it correctly. The code averages over seeds first and thresholds second, which is the definition stated above. The other order would change 28 of the 55 cells that have a defined r*, in both directions, and would additionally invent two finite values where the correct answer is "never recovered": in _sigma4.0 at d = 0.50 the per-seed thresholds are {1.0, undefined, undefined}, and dropping the undefined seeds would report r* = 1.0 where the seed-mean curve never crosses the bar at all. That is a censoring bias that would systematically understate r*.
Consequence for how uncertainty should be reported. Because per-seed thresholds are not averaged, there is no standard error on r* to quote. The honest uncertainty is the per-seed threshold range, and for some cells that range is wide: _beta_0.30 at d = 1.5 has per-seed thresholds of {0.1, 0.3, 0.75}, a sevenfold spread across three seeds on an eight-point grid.

Three things that are correct but fragile, and should carry a caveat

FindingDetail
One r* value is decided by one part in 44,000 _sigma6.0 at d = 0.30 reports r* = 0.20. Its mean final F1 clears the bar by 9.8e-06. The curve is non-monotone right there: r = 0.30 fails. One more epoch, a different seed or a different batch order would move it to 0.50. Report it as “0.2, marginal” or not at all.
The v1 main sweep has a saturated bar In synth_distance_sweep the ceiling is exactly 1.000 at every distance. That is not an error, but it means r* there is scored against a bar that is both fixed and perfect. It is the least informative ceiling in the whole project, and it is the sweep whose r*(d) curve was the originally reported law.
Ceilings have no error bar The ceiling in every sweep is computed once, from a fixed RNG that does not depend on the sweep seeds. It is a single unreplicated draw. r* is a threshold against it, so all of r*'s seed variation is in the numerator and none is in the bar.

Two structural notes worth carrying

Some arms are re-runs of the same configuration, not independent replicates. The synth_v2_distance rows at alpha = 0.5 are byte-identical to the alpha = 0.5 block of synth_v2_alpha_sweep, and synth_v2_beta_0.50 at alpha = 1.0 is identical to the alpha = 1.0 block of the alpha sweep. All four beta directories share an identical d = 0 row, since beta has no effect at zero distance. Do not count these as separate evidence.
The deepest recorded "dip" is not a dip. The largest single-run dip depth in the v2 distance arm (0.1202, at d = 0.00, r = 0.20, seed 42) has minimum F1 equal to final F1. That run did not fall and recover; it declined monotonically and finished at its worst point. At d = 0 with a flat ceiling that is optimisation noise. It strengthens rather than weakens the noise-floor reading, but the mechanism should be named rather than folded into a dip statistic.

Reproduce it

module load Miniforge3 && eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)" conda activate /work/ah2lab/LiamK/conda_envs/plm_dynamics # for each sweep dir: read sweep_results.csv, group by (distance, alpha, ood_frac), # take the seed mean of final_f1, then the first r whose mean >= 0.9 * ceiling

Earlier entries

Work before 12 August is catalogued run by run on the experiment catalogue page, and audited against filesystem timestamps in section 21g of that page. This ledger begins where that audit left off.

Conventions used here. Every entry gives the question, the exact command, the job ID, the output path and the verdict. Runs that were discarded are recorded with the reason. Anything that could not be verified is stated as unverified rather than omitted.

The record

Open work

The backlog: what needs no new compute, what needs a GPU, and what needs a decision

What has not been done, why it matters, and what it would take. The lab ledger records what was run; this page records what was not. Items are grouped by what stands between them and an answer, and ranked within each group by value per unit of effort.

Every item states what result would undermine the current story, not only what would support it. Several of these are expected to return a null, and are listed anyway because an unasked question is a weaker position than an answered one.

Tier 1: ready to run

No new embeddings, no GPU, everything already on disk. The whole tier is well under two hours of CPU.

T1.1Is retention just Pfam coverage? ready to run

Why it is firstThis is the strongest competing explanation for the headline result and it is currently invisible in the document. A pre-screen already gives Spearman +0.86 (p = 1e-4, n = 14) between retention and the fraction of target proteins whose Pfam the source has already seen.
QuestionIs the bacterial against non-bacterial split simply 'how much of the target's Pfam vocabulary the source already contains'? And is that a better predictor than the whole embedding-geometry battery?
Inputsec_swissprot/raw/ec_swissprot_raw.tsv (column pfam is a semicolon-separated multi-Pfam list, mean 1.62 per protein, and only the first ever reached metadata.tsv), ec_rstar/ladder/rstar_summary_pair.csv, ec_rstar/rstar_allpairs_flat.csv, ec_rstar/rstar_vs_distance_P500_joined.csv
MethodFor every ordered pair compute three coverage statistics: the fraction of target proteins with at least one Pfam seen in the source; the fraction whose Pfam is seen in the source with the same EC label, which is the transferable-homologue version; and the median count of source proteins sharing a Pfam with each target protein. Spearman each against retention at n = 14 and n = 209, then partial the geometry predictors on coverage and vice versa, with a group-level permutation null.
What would undermine usIf coverage beats proxy-A distance and the geometry predictors go non-significant when partialled on it, the story becomes 'retention is homologue availability and the geometry is a proxy for it'. That is a substantial reframing, and it is consistent with the subspace result.
What would support usThe archaea are the decisive case: coverage 0.79 but retention 0.34 to 0.47, well below the coverage trend line. If geometry survives partialling there, the current account is strengthened and we gain a strong negative control.
CostAbout 5 minutes. Null risk low: the marginal effect is already confirmed, the open question is the direction of the partials.

T1.2Extend the geometry-to-threshold correlation from 14 pairs to 209 ready to run

QuestionEvery correlation table in rstar_vs_distance_P500.json reports n = 14, because only the gammaproteobacteria-source rows were ever correlated. About 195 of the 211 rows in that file have never been analysed. Do the predictors hold when the source is not held fixed?
Inputsec_rstar/rstar_vs_distance_P500_joined.csv, 211 rows by 45 columns, which already carries lr_retained, lr_rstar, all geo_* and all the label-free distances
MethodRepeat the existing Spearman and partial-given-K protocol on all 209 pairs. Because pairs share sources and targets, add a within-source ranking analysis and a double permutation that permutes source and target labels separately. Exclude the BLAST predictors, which are populated only for the 14 gamma rows.
What would undermine usIf the correlations collapse off the gamma row, the label-free predictor claim is an n = 14 result with 24 predictors tested, and the file itself warns that about 1.2 false positives are expected by chance. That would be the single most important caveat to surface.
Cost2 minutes, or 10 with a proper double permutation.

T1.3Mine the adaptation dip from 3,200 unused per-run rows ready to run

Questionrstar_runs_*.csv holds start_f1, min_f1 and dip_depth for about 3,200 real adaptation runs. None of those columns survives into rstar_summary_*.csv. Does the transient collapse carry information beyond r*?
MethodUse a normalised dip, (start − min) / start, to remove the ceiling artefact that produces a spurious positive correlation. Per target, find the smallest mixing fraction at which the mean normalised dip falls inside the r = 1.0 noise band, and compare that to r*budget by Kendall tau.
Why it could matterIf the two agree, there is a second estimator of the same threshold that needs no target-only ceiling, which would sidestep the single largest source of error in this project. If they disagree, that is a clean statement that the dip and the threshold are different phenomena.
Already knownMean dip falls monotonically with r: 0.227, 0.198, 0.171, 0.128, 0.103, 0.068, 0.050, 0.042. So the axis is real; only the agreement with r* is open.
Cost5 minutes. Moderate null risk on the agreement.

T1.4A within-group null for retention ready to run

QuestionRetention has no zero point. Bacteroidetes reads 1.001, but nobody has measured what the statistic gives when there is no taxonomic shift at all.
MethodInside gammaproteobacteria, split organisms into two disjoint halves, first at random and then by genus and by order using lineage_ids, with source and target sizes matched to a real cross-group pair. Report the retention distribution over about 20 partitions, and repeat inside firmicutes and vertebrata.
Why it mattersIf random within-group retention sits at 0.97 to 1.00, the 8 bacterial targets span 'essentially no shift' to 'real shift' and the 6 non-bacterial ones are unambiguously outside the null. If it comes in at 0.85, several bacterial targets are indistinguishable from no shift and the 8-against-6 framing has to be restated as a null band.
CostAbout 20 minutes. Null risk very low: a number is guaranteed and we do not have one.

T1.5Cross-arm error bars on the retention ranking ready to run

QuestionHow much of the retention ordering is an artefact of the specific arm?
Already partly knownThe domain separation holds in every arm, but the within-bacteria ranking does not: bacteroidetes moves 1.001 to 0.583 and spirochaetes 0.983 to 0.669 between the _pair and _sizematched arms, while betaproteobacteria barely moves.
MethodBuild a 14 by 6 matrix of retention per target per arm across all four ladder arms plus ladder_fast and the superseded run, compute pairwise Kendall tau, and test the 8-against-6 separation in each arm. Report per-target minimum and maximum as an error bar.
Why it mattersThe honest headline is 'the domain split is robust, the within-bacteria ranking is not'. Presenting the ranking without that error bar is the vulnerable part of the current write-up.
Cost5 minutes. No null risk: the outcome is already known to be informative.

T1.6Protein-level identity against protein-level correctness ready to run

Questionec_rstar/seqid/hits_*.tsv holds 107,799 raw BLAST hits that were collapsed to 15 summary rows. At the level of an individual protein, is it classified correctly zero-shot because it has a close homologue in the source?
MethodTake each query's best hit identity, train one gamma-source probe at EC level 3, record per-protein correctness, and fit correctness against identity within each target group and pooled. Also compare against transferring the best hit's own EC label.
What would support usA flat relationship within group, meaning group identity predicts correctness but per-protein identity does not, would be strong evidence that the representation rather than pairwise homology carries the transfer.
CostAbout 15 minutes.

T1.7Which enzyme chemistry actually survives transfer ready to run

QuestionIs low retention uniform across EC top-level classes, or concentrated in the classes whose prevalence differs most between domains? Hydrolases are 37 to 40% of eukaryotic proteins against 15 to 21% of bacterial ones; ligases run the other way.
MethodNothing on disk stores per-class F1, so re-run the zero-shot and ceiling steps only, dump f1_score(average=None), and regress class-level retention on the prevalence difference for that class.
Why it mattersIf the loss concentrates in classes rare in the source, the mechanism is label-marginal shift rather than representational shift. If it is uniform, the representational account is strengthened. Either way it produces the biologically interesting sentence the thesis currently cannot write.
Cost20 to 30 minutes.

T1.8Close the length and composition confound ready to run

QuestionDoes protein length confound taxonomic distance? length and organism_id exist in the raw file and have never been used anywhere.
Already knownMedian length against retention is non-significant (ρ = −0.32, p = 0.27). Length-KS and EC-composition divergence both give ρ = −0.73.
The dissociation to reportCrenarchaeota and euryarchaeota are the shortest groups in the corpus, with near-bacterial EC composition, yet retention 0.343 and 0.469. Length cannot be the mechanism.
Cost15 minutes. High null risk by design. Run it to close the question, not to find an effect.

Tier 2: needs new compute

GPU time or a long CPU job. Each is a few hours at most.

T2.1Extend the two-model replication to the archaea needs new compute

WhyThe ESM-2 replication covers four domains and no archaea. Crenarchaeota and euryarchaeota are the two groups that break every simple explanation, so they are exactly the ones the replication is missing.
MethodEmbed 5,000 proteins from each of crenarchaeota, euryarchaeota and a few more groups with ESM-2 650M using src/embed_esm2_ec.py, then rerun subspace_plm2.slurm. Better still, embed the full 14-target ladder and repeat the retention measurement itself, not only the subspace geometry.
Cost20 minutes per 20,000 sequences on one A100. The full ladder is about 2 hours.

T2.2BLAST for all 210 pairs needs new compute

WhyEvery pident correlation rests on 14 points from a single source group, because BLAST was only ever run out of gammaproteobacteria. The document already flags any identity-against-r* claim as suggestive until this is done.
CostAbout a day of CPU. The most quotable axis in the project is the least well supported.

T2.3A matched BLAST against embedding comparison needs new compute

WhyAn uncontrolled comparison currently puts BLAST nearest-neighbour ahead of the embedding on 11 of 14 groups. That comparison is not matched: different protein samples, different label sets, different F1 denominators, so it is not presented as a result. But in ProteInfer's own clustered split BLAST beats the CNN, and in CARE BLASTp equals or beats CLEAN on 3 of 4 splits. If homology search wins on equal terms, that reframes the chapter.
CostHours. This is the single most consequential unrun experiment in the project.

Tier 3: needs a decision before it is worth starting

Each of these changes something that other results depend on, so none should be started unilaterally.

T3.1Should the generator move to whitened coordinates? needs a decision

The case forMeasured on 13 August: α goes from ρ = −0.026 to −0.740 under whitening, negative in 15 of 15 source groups, and the subspace experiment shows the signal and nuisance split only holds in whitened coordinates. The generator is a model of whitened embeddings that has always been compared against raw ones.
The case againstgenerate_synthetic_v2.py has been unchanged since 21 July at 17:02, and every v2 sweep in this document depends on that stability. Changing the coordinate system invalidates the comparability of every existing v2 result.
The decisionEither rebuild and re-sweep, accepting that the July results become historical, or keep the generator and report the whitened measurement as a property of real embeddings that the generator does not capture. Not both.

T3.2Drop β, or keep it with the caveat? needs a decision

What is settledIn raw coordinates β is robustly the wrong sign, partial ρ = +0.414, positive in 14 of 15 groups. Whitening flips the partial to −0.648, so the diagnosis was right, but whitened β has a median of 0.017 and no marginal correlation at all.
The standing criterionThe document's own rule was 'if β still does not go negative it should be dropped rather than defended'. It goes negative only conditionally and is unusable either way.
The decisionRemove β from the generator's knob set and from the realism scorecard, or retain it as a historical quantity with the caveat attached everywhere it appears.

T3.3Add the missing generator terms needs a decision

The three known mismatchesProcrustes disparity is 12 to 32 times too small and is independently the 4th best damage predictor. Intrinsic dimension is 8.6 times off. Class-covariance heterogeneity is 3.2 times off, with a cheap fix available, a per-class random rotation of the covariance.
Why it needs a decisionEach addition changes the universe and therefore every existing sweep, exactly as in T3.1. They should be decided together with it, not separately.

T3.4Recompute the synthetic r*(d) curve with the repaired estimator needs a decision

WhyTwo of the six estimator defects found in August live in the synthetic sweep's own code: adaptation running for a single pass, and a ceiling trained on more data than the pool. Its 'never recovers' points beyond d = 0.75 may be artefacts.
Why it needs a decisionIt would supersede the r*(d) law as currently reported.

T3.5The oracle's within-family label distribution needs a decision

The unresolved conflictReal data wants purity 69% and coverage 2.98 simultaneously, which implies a heavy-tailed within-family label distribution. The oracle's argmax produces roughly balanced classes, so it can only buy purity by having very few classes. The proposed fix, a Zipf-like distribution within each family, has never been implemented.
What it would unlockThe only route to a synthetic dataset with EC-like rather than Pfam-like labels, which is the empty cell in the coverage matrix and the reason every synthetic result here is a homology result.

Tier 4: writing, not compute

Positioning changes that follow from the 13 August literature check.

T4.1Reframe the subspace finding against the erasure literature writing, not compute

What to changeThe raw-against-whitened result should be presented as confirmation and quantification in a new domain, not as a discovery. The mechanism is anticipated in 1983 for discriminant analysis, demonstrated for transformer embeddings in 2021, and formalised by concept-erasure theory in 2023, whose erasure operator whitens, projects and unwhitens.
The claim that survivesThe raw low-rank centroid subspace, which is the natural thing to build and is what a published attribute-removal method builds, retains essentially none of the EC-discriminative signal in protein embeddings, while the whitened subspace at the same rank retains nearly all of it. Four domains, two encoders.

T4.2Cite and rebut the counter-evidence writing, not compute

WhatA 2025 study using cross-species complementation reports ESM-C embeddings beating a sequence-identity baseline 21 of 22 against 19 of 22. It is the strongest published argument that these embeddings carry function beyond homology.
HowCite it and weigh it on sample size: 22 triplets and a two-protein margin. A reader who knows the field will raise it, so it should be addressed rather than omitted.

T4.3Report displacement in both metrics writing, not compute

WhyA fixed Euclidean displacement is not a fixed intervention. Measured directly, two gaps in raw coordinates is 8 to 10 within-class standard deviations inside the function subspace but 17 to 29 outside it, so part of the raw-against-whitened contrast restates the change of metric.
StatusThe diagnostic is already recorded in every run from job 47447997 as mag_in_within_class_sd. It needs to appear in the write-up, and the displacement result should stay demoted to the weakest of the three.

Keeping this page useful

Convention. An item leaves this page only when it has an entry in the lab ledger and a row in the catalogue, including when the answer is a null. Items that are abandoned rather than answered should be moved to a closed section with the reason, not deleted, so that the same question is not proposed twice.
If only one thing gets done, make it T1.1. It is five minutes, it uses data already on disk, and it is the only item that could change what the headline result means.

Reference

Concepts

Every term used in this document, defined in one place

Throughout this document, a term with a dotted underline can be hovered for a one-line definition without leaving the page, and clicked to arrive here. Nothing on this page is a result; it is the vocabulary. Where a concept has a fuller treatment elsewhere, each entry links straight to it.

111 entries

The quantities this project measures

Everything the project reports is one of these. If a chart has a number on it, the number is defined here.

budget

The fixed number of proteins a scientist can afford to label by hand. Held constant across the whole sweep, so that changing the mixing fraction changes composition and not size.

also: labelling budgetFull entry → Measures: r* by budget

ceiling

The score of a fresh model trained only on the new group's own data. What is achievable if you ignore transfer entirely. r* is defined as a fraction of it, which is exactly why a ceiling that moves for the wrong reasons corrupts r*.

Full entry → Measures: ceiling

dip depth

How far a curve falls below its own starting score. Only meaningful against the noise floor: a dip smaller than the floor is not evidence of anything.

Full entry → Measures: dip depth

macro-F1

The score behind every number here. Each class is scored separately and the scores are averaged, so a rare class counts as much as a common one. 0 is useless, 1 is perfect.

also: macro F1Full entry → Background: classifiers and macro-F1

mixing fraction (r)

What share of the fixed labelling budget is drawn from the new organisms rather than the old ones. Sweeping r from 0 to 1 is what produces a recovery curve.

also: pool composition

negative transfer (the dip)

Adding correct new training data makes performance worse before it gets better. The curve dips below where it started. This is the phenomenon the whole project exists to measure.

also: negative transfer, the dipFull entry → The recovery threshold and the dip

noise floor

How much damage extra training does when there is no shift at all (distance = 0). Any dip at or below this level is measurement noise, not negative transfer.

r* (the recovery threshold)

The headline quantity. Of a fixed labelling budget, the smallest fraction that must come from the new organisms before the model reaches 90% of what it could achieve. Low r* means transfer is cheap; high r* means you must label almost everything yourself.

also: r*, recovery thresholdFull entry → The recovery threshold and the dip

retention

Zero-shot score divided by the ceiling: the fraction of achievable performance that transfer gives you for free, before labelling anything. On real EC data this turned out to be far more stable than r*, and is now the headline.

Full entry → Measures: retention

zero-shot

The score on the new group having seen zero examples from it. What you get for free.

Full entry → Measures: zero-shot

Machine learning

The vocabulary of training a classifier, at the level needed to read the results.

Adam

The optimiser used here: a version of gradient descent that gives each weight its own step size based on how it has been behaving.

Full entry → Background: the classifier, layer by layer

adaptation

Continuing to train an already-trained model on a pool that mixes old and new data, so it adjusts to the new organisms.

also: domain adaptationFull entry → Measures: the MLP and the adaptation loop

attention

The mechanism letting a language model weigh every position in a sequence against every other, so a residue's representation depends on its context.

also: transformerFull entry → Background: inside ESM-C

batch normalisation

A layer that rescales its inputs using statistics of the data it has seen. Those statistics come from the source data, which is why recalibrating them alone is a genuine adaptation method.

also: BatchNorm, batch normFull entry → Background: the classifier, layer by layer

classifier

A function that takes a protein and outputs a guess at its label. Here: 960 numbers in, one of roughly 30 to 112 enzyme classes out.

also: classifier / model

cross-entropy

The particular loss used here. It punishes confident wrong answers far more harshly than hesitant ones, and the punishment grows without limit as confidence in the truth goes to zero.

Full entry → Background: the classifier, layer by layer

decision boundary

The invisible surface a classifier draws through space, separating 'I would call this class A' from 'class B'.

also: decision boundariesFull entry → Background: classifiers and macro-F1

dropout

Deliberately switching off a random share of the network during each training step, so it cannot lean too hard on any one path.

Full entry → Background: the classifier, layer by layer

epoch

A batch is a handful of examples used for one nudge; an epoch is one full pass through the training data.

also: mini-batchFull entry → Background: how a model learns

forward pass

Running one protein through the network to get a prediction, before any learning happens.

Full entry → Background: how a model learns

gradient descent

Work out, for every internal number, whether nudging it up would raise or lower the loss, then nudge every one of them slightly downhill. Repeat. Backpropagation is the trick that gets all those slopes at once.

also: gradient, backpropagation, backpropFull entry → Background: how a model learns

learning rate

How big each downhill nudge is. Too small and training crawls; too large and it overshoots and never settles.

Full entry → Background: how a model learns

linear probe

The simplest possible classifier: one straight boundary. Used as a cheap stand-in. It gives different numbers than the MLP, so results from the two are never mixed.

Full entry → Measures: the linear probe

loss

A single number saying how wrong the model's guess was. Training is the process of making it smaller.

Full entry → Background: how a model learns

masked-residue pretraining

How the protein language model was trained: hide a residue, make the model guess it, repeat over millions of sequences. It was never shown an EC number.

Full entry → Background: inside ESM-C

mean pooling

Averaging a model's per-residue outputs into one vector for the whole protein. How a sequence of any length becomes a fixed 960 numbers.

Full entry → Background: inside ESM-C

MLP

A plain, small neural network. The one used throughout: 960 inputs, then 512, then 256, then one output per class.

also: multi-layer perceptronFull entry → Background: the classifier, layer by layer

optimal transport

An adaptation method that finds the cheapest way to move one cloud of points onto another. Best of all methods on synthetic data and worst on every real shift tested, which is why the synthetic-to-real gap matters.

also: optimal-transport alignment, OT

ReLU

A bend applied between layers: negative values become zero, positive ones pass through. Without it, stacking layers would be no more powerful than a single layer.

Full entry → Background: the classifier, layer by layer

seed

The number fixing a run's randomness. Repeating a run at several seeds shows how much of a result is real and how much is luck.

also: seeds

softmax

The last step, turning the network's raw scores into probabilities that add to one.

Full entry → Background: the classifier, layer by layer

train / test split

Hiding some examples during training and scoring on those. Otherwise the model can memorise instead of learn, and you would never know.

training

Showing the model examples with known answers and nudging its internal numbers until its guesses improve.

Full entry → Background: how a model learns

warm start

Beginning adaptation from the trained source model's weights rather than from scratch. The alternative to throwing the source model away.

Full entry → Background: how a model learns

Maths and geometry

Embeddings are points in a 960-dimensional space, so most of the argument is geometry.

anisotropy

Spread out more in some directions than others: a cigar rather than a ball. Real embeddings are strongly anisotropic, and that turned out to matter enormously.

also: anisotropic

Bayes accuracy

The best any classifier could possibly do given how the classes actually overlap. A hard limit set by geometry, not by the model. Used to show a task got easier or harder for purely geometric reasons.

also: Bayes error

centroid

The average position of all points sharing a label: where a family lives.

also: centroids

covariance

The full description of a cloud's shape: how much it spreads in every direction, and how those directions relate to each other.

dimension

How many numbers are in the list. This space has 960.

also: dimensions, dimensionalFull entry → Properties of 960-dimensional space

effective rank

How many directions the data really uses. Nominally 960 here, but effectively three to eleven: nearly flat in all the rest.

Full entry → Properties of 960-dimensional space

Gaussian

The bell-curve blob shape: most points near the centre, fewer further out.

also: normal distribution, Gaussians

Gaussian mixture

A universe built as a set of bell-curve blobs, one per family. What the synthetic generator draws its points from.

also: GMMFull entry → Constructing the synthetic universe

injective

One-to-one: no two different inputs give the same output, so nothing is destroyed on the way through.

intrinsic dimension

How many dimensions the data really occupies locally, as opposed to the 960 it is written in. Close cousin of effective rank.

isometry

A move that preserves every distance exactly. Sliding and rotating qualify; stretching and squashing do not. Enforcing this is what separates generator v2 from v1.

also: isometries, isometricFull entry → The isometry rule, and three failed constructions

norm

The length of a vector, written with double bars. In two dimensions it is Pythagoras; in 960 it is the same sum with 960 terms.

Full entry → Background: distance, spread and direction

orthogonal

At right angles. In high dimensions almost every pair of random directions is nearly perpendicular, which has consequences throughout.

also: perpendicularFull entry → Properties of 960-dimensional space

orthogonal basis

A set of mutually perpendicular directions that spans a space: a coordinate system, possibly rotated.

PCA

Principal component analysis: the same computation as SVD, under a different name.

Full entry → Background: distance, spread and direction

power law

A quantity that falls off as one over k to some power: a few big values, then a long tail of small ones. Describes both family sizes and the spread across directions.

also: power-law

projection

The shadow a vector casts onto a subspace: the part of a move that happens inside those directions.

rotation

Spinning everything rigidly about a point. An isometry, so it moves families without changing any distance between them.

standard deviation

How spread out points are around their centre. Written sigma, and in the same units as distance; variance is its square. Large sigma means a fat, diffuse cloud.

also: varianceFull entry → Background: distance, spread and direction

subspace

A smaller space living inside a bigger one, like a flat sheet inside a room. The 960-dimensional space here contains a much smaller subspace that carries the label information.

also: subspacesFull entry → Signal and nuisance subspaces

SVD

Finds the natural axes of a cloud of points, ordered widest to narrowest, each with a number for how much spread lies along it. Same computation as PCA. The name explains nothing.

also: singular value decomposition, singular value, singular valuesFull entry → Background: distance, spread and direction

unit vector

A vector of length exactly one. Used when direction matters but distance does not.

vector

An ordered list of numbers. A protein's embedding is a vector of 960 of them. Also usable as an arrow from one point to another.

The shift

A 'shift' is what happens to the data when you move to a new set of organisms. These words describe its size, its shape and its direction.

alpha

What fraction of the movement every family shares. At 1 the whole cloud slides rigidly and the families keep their arrangement; at 0 each family goes its own way and the arrangement breaks. It is the knob that decides whether a shift is merely displacement or genuine rearrangement.

Full entry → The alpha knob

B (the function subspace)

The directions along which enzyme classes differ most, found by SVD of the class centroids. It is a place in space, not a quantity: B is the road, beta is what fraction of the journey was on it.

also: function subspaceFull entry → Measures: beta and the function subspace

B-perpendicular

Everything not in B: the remaining directions. Displacement out here predicts damage about twice as strongly as displacement inside B, which was the clue that B is simply the roomier half of the space.

also: B-perp

beta

What fraction of a move landed inside the directions that carry function. Intended as a damage knob. Its meaning did not survive testing on real embeddings, and it is the project's most reversed claim.

Full entry → The beta knob

centroid configuration

The whole set of class centroids considered as one shape: a constellation. Preserving the configuration means the constellation keeps its shape even if it moves or spins.

concept shift

The rule itself changed. Classes have rearranged relative to each other, so the old boundary is now genuinely in the wrong place, not just moved.

Full entry → Measures: concept shift

conditioned shift

Read the bar as 'holding fixed'. TAX|EC means move across taxonomy while holding the enzyme class constant; EC|DOM means move between enzyme classes within one taxonomic domain.

Full entry → Measures: shift vocabulary

covariate shift

The data moved, but the rule linking data to label did not. Everything slides together, so the old boundary is merely displaced rather than wrong.

Full entry → Measures: covariate shift

d (the distance knob)

How far the synthetic target universe is moved from the source. The axis along which every synthetic recovery curve is swept.

Full entry → The shift: d, alpha and beta

derangement

A shuffle where nothing stays put: every item ends up somewhere that is not its own place. Generator v1 moved each family toward another family's position using one of these, and that choice is what bent its ceiling.

Full entry → Ceiling behaviour across the three configurations

differential component

What is left after subtracting the shared part: each class's own idiosyncratic move, the individual bird's wobble relative to the flock. This does rearrange the classes, which is why it breaks the old boundary.

also: family-specific part, differential motionFull entry → The shift: d, alpha and beta

displacement vector

One arrow per class: from where that class sat in the source to where it sits in the target. It moved this far, in this direction.

also: displacement

excess

Within-move minus cross-move. The honest measure of whether a shift is structured, because it subtracts the baseline you would get from unrelated moves.

point reflection

Flipping every point through the origin, which is what a 180-degree rotation does. The furthest a rotation can move things before it starts coming back.

rigid translation

Sliding everything by the same vector without rotating or resizing. Preserves every distance.

shared component

The part of the move every class has in common: the average of all the displacement vectors. A flock of birds flying north. Because every class moves identically, their positions relative to each other do not change.

also: shared translationFull entry → The shift: d, alpha and beta

signal and nuisance subspaces

The directions that carry the label, versus the directions that carry everything else. In the generator the signal subspace is declared and all its directions are equally wide; on real data it is estimated, and its directions differ in width elevenfold. That contrast is why beta works in simulation and fails on real data.

also: signal subspace, nuisance subspaceFull entry → Signal and nuisance subspaces

within-move vs cross-move

Within-move fixes one move and asks whether it looks the same in different contexts. Cross-move pools across different moves, which average toward zero even under perfect structure. Comparing the two incorrectly is a documented error here.

also: within-move, cross-moveFull entry → Measures: shift vocabulary

Comparing synthetic data to real data

The measures used to ask whether the generated universe resembles the real one.

additivity

Whether two effects simply add. If family membership moves a protein one way and enzyme class moves it another, is the combined position just the sum?

energy distance

Another label-free cloud-versus-cloud distance, with no tuning parameter to argue about.

Full entry → Measures: label-free distances

feature Wasserstein

A distance built by comparing each feature's distribution separately. Tested as the distance axis and rejected: it is not monotone in the true distance.

Full entry → Measures: label-free distances

Fréchet distance

Treats each cloud as a single bell shape and compares those. The same idea as the FID score used for image generators. Unstable here: 960 dimensions estimated from a few thousand samples.

also: Frechet distanceFull entry → Measures: label-free distances

hubness

In high dimensions a few points end up being nearest neighbour to an unreasonable number of others. How much this happens is a fingerprint of the geometry.

kNN label consistency

Take a protein's nearest neighbours and ask what fraction share its label. A direct measure of how cleanly labels cluster.

MMD

Maximum mean discrepancy: a way to measure how different two clouds of points are without needing any labels.

also: maximum mean discrepancyFull entry → Measures: label-free distances

principal angles

The set of angles between two subspaces, measuring how much they overlap. Small angles mean the two occupy much the same directions.

Full entry → Measures: principal angles

probe logit spread

How much a shift moves each class's score in a linear probe, relative to normal variation. An estimate of damage taken from the classifier itself rather than guessed.

Procrustes disparity

How much a constellation rearranges, ignoring any overall sliding, spinning or resizing. Zero means the same shape moved around; large means genuinely reshuffled. It catches what alpha, beta and distance are all blind to.

Full entry → Measures: Procrustes disparity

proxy-A distance

Train a classifier to guess 'source or target?' from the embedding alone. If it cannot, the two domains overlap. On protein embeddings it is nearly saturated.

Full entry → Measures: label-free distances

sequence identity

What percentage of two proteins' amino acids match once aligned. The standard biological measure of relatedness, and the best available predictor of transfer difficulty.

Full entry → The real-EC run

whitening

Rescaling every direction by its own spread, so one unit means the same thing everywhere. Moving 100 units of height is enormous; 100 units of income is nothing. The z-score idea applied to every direction at once.

also: whitened, whitened unitsFull entry → Measures: whitening

Statistics

How claims here are tested, and the ways such tests go wrong.

ablation

Deliberately removing a component to see whether anything depends on it. If performance is unchanged, the component was not load-bearing.

also: ablate

censoring

A measurement that never happened because it ran off the end of the scale, e.g. the bar was never reached at any r. Dropping these silently biases results toward the easy cases.

also: censoredFull entry → Measures: censoring

matched control

A comparison run built to differ from the real one in exactly one respect, so that any difference in outcome can only be caused by that respect.

also: matched controlsFull entry → Measures: matched controls

min_n

The minimum number of proteins a class must have before it is included at all. Stops centroids being computed from three data points.

multiple comparisons

Test twenty-four things and one or two will look significant by luck alone. You have to say how many you tested.

Full entry → Measures: multiple comparisons

p-value

The chance of seeing a pattern this strong if there were really no pattern at all. Small means unlikely to be a fluke.

permutation null

Shuffle the labels many times, re-measure each time, and see how often chance beats the real result. An honest p-value when the data are not independent.

Full entry → Measures: group-level permutation null

shuffled-label control

Re-running with the labels randomly reassigned, to establish what score is achievable with no real signal at all.

Spearman's rho

Does one quantity rise when another does? +1 is perfectly together, 0 unrelated, -1 perfectly opposite. Spearman uses rank order only, so it does not care about the exact shape.

also: correlation, SpearmanFull entry → Measures: Spearman's rho

Proteins and data

The biology, the labels, and the datasets.

EC number

A four-level code for the reaction an enzyme performs. Only the first three levels are used here, which is the level of the chemistry rather than the exact substrate.

also: EC, EC level 3, EC L3Full entry → Proteins, EC numbers and Pfam families

embedding

The list of numbers a protein language model outputs for a protein. Every protein here is 960 numbers, and everything downstream is geometry on those numbers.

also: embeddingsFull entry → Embeddings

ESM-2

An earlier protein language model, outputting 1280 numbers per protein. Used as the independent second model, to test whether findings are properties of proteins or merely of ESM-C.

Full entry → Measures: ESM-2 650M

ESM-C

The protein language model used for most of this project. Outputs 960 numbers per protein.

also: ESM-C 300MFull entry → Background: inside ESM-C

homology

Shared ancestry. What Pfam measures, and the thing the model may be quietly relying on when it appears to predict function.

also: homologousFull entry → Proteins, EC numbers and Pfam families

metagenome

All the DNA scooped from an environment at once, without isolating organisms. The motivating use case for the whole question.

Full entry → Motivation

Pfam family

A group of proteins descended from a common ancestor: related by ancestry, not by job. Every synthetic result here labels by family, which is why the distinction from EC matters so much.

also: PfamFull entry → Proteins, EC numbers and Pfam families

protein language model

A model trained on millions of protein sequences that turns a sequence into a vector. It was never shown a functional label during training, which is what makes its embeddings a fair starting point.

also: PLMFull entry → Background: inside ESM-C

purity and coverage

Two properties of a manufactured label space that pull against each other: how consistently one family maps to one label, versus how many families a label spans. The conflict between them is unresolved.

also: purityFull entry → What the oracle was tuned on

Swiss-Prot

The manually reviewed portion of the UniProt protein database. Small, clean, and trustworthy in its annotations.

also: SwissProtFull entry → Datasets: ec_swissprot

taxonomic group

A branch of the tree of life: bacteria, archaea, plants, vertebrates. The axis the data is shifted along.

also: taxonomy, taxonomic

taxonomic ladder

A set of target groups ordered by how far they sit from the training data, from close bacteria out to vertebrates and plants. The real-data equivalent of turning the distance knob.

also: taxonomy ladderFull entry → Datasets: taxonomy_ladder

the oracle

A frozen, never-trained network used by generator v0 to assign labels. Because it labelled source and target alike, the dip was structurally impossible, and removing it was what made the project measurable.

also: oracle labelsFull entry → The oracle, and its removal

TrEMBL

The automatically annotated portion of UniProt. Vastly larger than Swiss-Prot and far noisier, which makes the move from one to the other a realistic test of transfer.

Full entry → Swiss-Prot to TrEMBL

Datasets

Every body of data used anywhere here, how it was built, and what it cannot answer

Every number in this document was computed on one of the seven bodies of data below. Each entry says how it was built, what labels it carries, where it lives, and what it cannot be used for. Anything elsewhere in the document that names a dataset links here.

The one distinction to keep straight. Three of these are synthetic, generated by code, where the true answer is known by construction. Four are real Swiss-Prot proteins embedded by a protein language model, where it is not. Mixing them is the single easiest way to misread this project, which is why every figure carries a badge.

ec_swissprot real EC Pfam

The current real dataset, and the basis of every result from 6 August onwards.

Why the rebuild mattered more than the size. The previous dataset had 5 taxonomic groups, giving 20 ordered pairs. A group-level permutation test over 5 groups has only 120 possible arrangements, so nothing could reach significance regardless of whether it was true. Fifteen groups give 210 pairs, and 9 of 12 damage predictors became significant immediately. The n = 20 against n = 210 comparison shows four predictors changing sign.
What it cannot answer. There is almost no natural functional novelty in it: gammaproteobacteria contains nearly every EC class at level 3 that any other group has, and nine of fourteen targets have zero classes that are absent from the source. Any functional-novelty result on this dataset is constructed by withholding classes, not observed.

Reference

Measures and statistics

Every quantity and statistic, with its definition and its known pitfalls

Every quantity this document reports, with its definition, the exact computation, and what can and cannot be concluded from it. Terms elsewhere in the document link here on first use.

One convention throughout. Every performance number is macro-F1, never accuracy. With class counts from 3 to 455 and heavy imbalance, accuracy is dominated by the largest classes and would flatter every result.

Outcome measures

Macro-F1

Compute precision and recall per class, take their harmonic mean per class, then average those unweighted across classes. A class with 15 proteins counts as much as one with 5,000.

F1_c = 2 · precision_c · recall_c / (precision_c + recall_c) macro-F1 = mean over classes of F1_c

Why it matters here. The rare classes are where a shift bites first, and macro-F1 is the measure that notices. It is also less forgiving: a model that abandons small classes entirely can still score well on accuracy and will collapse on macro-F1.

Zero-shot

The score of the source-trained model on the target test set, before any adaptation step. In the code this is f1s[0], the first point of the adaptation trajectory. Called baseline in the v1 outputs and zero_shot in v2; they are the same quantity.

Ceiling

A fresh model trained on target data only, with no source data involved. It answers "what is achievable if transfer is ignored entirely", and it is the bar that r* is scored against.

The ceiling has caused more errors in this project than anything else. It has been wrong in four separate ways: it moved with the distance knob in v1; it was computed on 40 times more data than the target had in the August ladder; it was scored against a full reservoir when the budget was 200; and in the v1 main sweep it was exactly 1.000 at every distance, a saturated and uninformative bar. Always report the ceiling next to the threshold.
It also carries no error bar. In every synthetic sweep the ceiling is computed once from a fixed RNG that does not depend on the sweep seeds. It is a single unreplicated draw, so all of r*'s seed variation sits in the numerator and none in the bar.

Retention

retention = zero-shot ÷ ceiling

The fraction of achievable performance that transfer gives you for free. This is the robust headline quantity of the project: it separates 8 bacterial targets (0.707 to 1.001) from 6 archaeal and eukaryotic ones (0.221 to 0.537) with no overlap, in three configurations and two estimators. It is continuous, needs no grid, and needs no threshold, which is exactly why it survives where r* does not.

A value above 1.0 is possible and occurs: bacteroidetes reads 1.001, meaning a foreign model trained on 20,000 gammaproteobacterial proteins beats a native model trained on all 1,264 bacteroidetes proteins that exist.

The recovery threshold, r*

r* = the smallest mixing fraction r on the grid at which the mean over seeds of the final target macro-F1 reaches 0.9 × ceiling undefined ("censored", "off-grid") if no r reaches it

The pool is fixed size P; a fraction r of it is target-labelled and the rest is source. The total number of labels never changes, only the composition. Grid: 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Method diagram on the measurement page.

Mean first, threshold second. The pipeline averages the seeds and then thresholds, which is the definition above. The other order, thresholding each seed and averaging the thresholds, changes 28 of the 55 defined cells and invents finite values where the correct answer is "never recovered". Verified against the raw per-run CSVs: 76 of 76 cells agree.
r* is fragile, and this is a result rather than a caveat. It is a threshold, on a bar that can move, read off an eight-point grid. Same data and same estimator give three different stories at three budgets. One published value clears its bar by 9.8e-06. Another moves by a grid step when only the list of distances requested changes. Report retention; quote r* only with its budget attached.

r*budget

The same threshold scored against 0.9 × a from-scratch model trained on P target proteins, rather than on the whole target reservoir. It exists because r* against the full ceiling is dominated by the budget: at P = 200 it censored 100% of 210 pairs. Because r = 1.0 reaches that bar by construction, this variant is essentially never censored.

The two are for different questions and must not share an axis. r*budget's bar rises with P, so it compares targets at a fixed budget. The absolute r*'s bar is fixed by the target reservoir, so it compares budgets, at the cost of being censored when P is small.

Dip depth, and negative transfer

dip depth = (target F1 at the start of adaptation) − (minimum target F1 during adaptation)

Computed per run, then averaged over seeds. It measures negative transfer: adding correct new training data making performance worse before it gets better. The dip happens inside an adaptation run, so charts that plot only endpoints cannot show it.

The comparison that matters. On real data every group falls 0.10 to 0.30 below its starting point at r = 0. In the synthetic v2 sweep the largest dips, 0.055 to 0.084, occur at d = 0.00 where there is no shift at all, so they are the noise floor. The generator was built to make negative transfer possible and does not reproduce it quantitatively.

Geometry of the shift

The gap, and the separation ratio

gap = mean Euclidean distance between class centroids, computed in the source domain only, over classes with at least min_n members

Currently 131 centroids giving 8,515 pairwise distances. It is the normaliser for every displacement magnitude, so every |v|/gap should be read against it. Alternatives, as multiples of the gap in use: median 0.95, 10th percentile 0.58, closest pair 0.24, pooled over all groups 1.09, Pfam centroids 1.29, two random proteins 1.57.

separation ratio = gap ÷ within-class σ = 1.11 EC classes sit about one within-class width apart

α, the shared-direction fraction

Each class has a displacement vector v_c from where it sits in the source to where it sits in the target. α is the mean pairwise cosine between those vectors. α = 1 means every class moves the same way, which is pure covariate shift; α = 0 means each class goes its own way, which is pure concept shift.

A within-move number and a cross-move number are not the same statistic. Pooling cosines across different moves averages toward zero even under perfect structure. The only interpretable quantity is excess = within minus cross. Getting this wrong produced the retracted claim that functional shift is unstructured. See the eight conditioned shifts.
α does not predict damage. Over 210 real pairs, ρ = +0.022, p = 0.87. It is a realism knob, not a cost measure.

β, and the function subspace B

B is a place: the top directions of the SVD of the source-domain EC centroids, holding 90% of between-class variance, currently 22 of 960. β is a number: the fraction of a shift's squared length that lands inside B.

β = ‖P_B(v)‖² ÷ ‖v‖² B is the road; β is what fraction of the journey was on it
β has the wrong sign on real data, ρ = +0.280, p = 0.0065 against retained F1. The explanation is geometric: SVD selects the widest directions by construction, so "inside B" mostly means "along a roomy axis". On real gammaproteobacteria the widest direction in B is 11.3 times the narrowest; in the generator that ratio is exactly 1.0. Full treatment in Q2 and the injection experiment.

Whitening

Rescaling every direction by its own standard deviation, so that one unit of movement means the same thing everywhere. It is the z-score idea generalised to every direction at once. Formally, using the SVD of the centred data, W = V · diag(√n / s).

Whitening decides the answer to the signal/nuisance question. In raw coordinates, deleting the function subspace costs nothing; in whitened coordinates the same deletion takes EC macro-F1 from 0.989 to 0.632, in four domains out of four. See the subspace experiment. Whitening on the source only is the honest choice, because at prediction time the target has not been seen.

Procrustes disparity

How much a constellation rearranges, after removing any overall translation, rotation and scaling. Zero means the same shape moved around; large means genuinely reshuffled. Computed as 1 − (sum of singular values of AᵀB)² for the two centred, normalised centroid configurations.

It is simultaneously the 4th best damage predictor (ρ = −0.634) and 32 times too small in the generator (0.026 against 0.322 to 0.835 real). Badly mismatched and strongly predictive is the profile of a missing knob.

Principal angles between subspaces

Given two orthonormal bases, the singular values of Qᵀ₁Q₂ are the cosines of the principal angles. A cosine of 1 means a shared direction; 0 means orthogonal. The mean over all angles summarises the overlap, and it must be read against a random-subspace null of the same dimensions, because two random subspaces in 960 dimensions already overlap somewhat.

Measured for the homology and function subspaces: 0.80 to 0.94 against nulls of 0.11 to 0.22.

Label-free distances

Computable before any target protein is labelled, which is what makes them useful for predicting a labelling budget in advance.

MeasureWhat it isVerdict here
MMD, RBF kernel Maximum mean discrepancy between the two point clouds, bandwidth by the median heuristic spans 10-fold across the ladder; one of the two usable metrics
Energy distance A kernel-free cloud-to-cloud distance with no bandwidth to argue about agrees closely with MMD
Fréchet distance Treats each cloud as one Gaussian and compares them; the FID idea unusable here: 3,000 samples in 960 dimensions leaves the covariance rank-deficient and the matrix square root untrustworthy
proxy-A distance Train a classifier to tell source from target; if it cannot, the domains overlap. It is the estimator in the Ben-David bound. saturated: 12 of 14 pairs exceed 1.83 of a maximum 2. Best theoretical claim, almost no dynamic range.
% sequence identity BLAST+ blastp, 1,500 queries per group against all 64,791 source proteins, best non-self hit the most quotable axis and the least discriminating over the range that matters: archaea, plants, fungi, insects and vertebrates all sit at 34 to 37%
Shared lineage nodes How much of the NCBI lineage the two groups share, 4 = same phylum down to 1 = different domain of life free, and it separates the ladder as well as anything else does

Statistics

Spearman's ρ

Correlation of ranks rather than values, so it is insensitive to the shape of the relationship and to outliers. Used throughout because most predictors here are monotone but not linear in damage.

Group-level permutation null

The single most important statistical choice in this project. The 210 ordered pairs come from 15 groups and are not independent: every group appears in 28 pairs, and both the predictor and the outcome are largely properties of the group. Permuting pairs would give wildly optimistic p-values. The null permutes whole groups and rebuilds the pair table, which preserves the dependence structure.

Two failures of this are on the record. With 5 groups there are only 120 arrangements, so nothing could reach significance whatever the truth. And an early version permuted both members of a pair, producing lookup keys that do not exist, silently rejecting nearly every draw and returning p ≈ 0 for predictors that had never been tested. It now holds the source fixed, permutes targets, reports nan when the null cannot be built, and uses (count+1)/(n+1) so p is never exactly zero.

Multiple comparisons

Twenty-four predictors are tested against each response, so roughly 1.2 false positives at p < 0.05 are expected per table by chance alone. This is stated in the output of every table and should be stated wherever one is quoted.

Censoring

A measurement that never happened because it ran off the end of the scale, here meaning r* never reached the bar at any mixing fraction. Dropping censored rows biases toward the easy cases. The censoring rate is itself a reported result: it falls from 78.9% to 15.9% as the budget goes from 500 to 2000, which is the direction the Ben-David theory predicts.

Matched controls

Two conclusions in this project were reversed by fixing a control, not by gathering more data. The claim that β causally damages function came from drawing the in-subspace direction from within B while drawing the off-subspace direction isotropically over all 960 dimensions. That contrast is "typical direction versus atypical direction", not "inside B versus outside B". With both drawn from the data covariance, β is protective. Separately, "hubness is 4.1 times off" evaporated to a ratio of 0.98 once the synthetic class count was matched to the real one.

Models and probes

The MLP, and the adaptation loop

960 → 512 → BatchNorm → ReLU → Dropout → 256 → ReLU → Dropout → K classes. 628,496 weights at K = 16. Adam, learning rate 0.001. Adaptation is a warm start from the source model, then training on the pool.

How long to adapt for is not a free choice. One pass measures the step count rather than the pool: on identical data, one warm-started pass scored 0.656 where 20 epochs from scratch scored 0.919. But a fixed 20 epochs overfits a 500-protein pool. Every model in the August ladder is therefore trained by the same rule: hold out a stratified 20% of its own training data, train up to 30 epochs, keep the best checkpoint by validation macro-F1.

The linear probe

Multinomial logistic regression on standardised features. Cheap enough to run over all 210 pairs, which the MLP is not. Its numbers are never pooled with the MLP's: a refit logistic regression gets no benefit from a warm start, so it needs more target data to clear the same bar. On the 14 shared targets the two agree on the qualitative call in 13 of 14 cases, and on retention they agree 14 of 14.

The scaler

Fitted on source training data only. Fitting it on the target is unsupervised domain adaptation in disguise and would silently shrink r*.

The oracle

A randomly initialised, never-trained neural network whose argmax defines a label. Used in v0 to manufacture a labelling rule with no biology in it. Removed in v1 because one global oracle means one global P(y|x), which makes the source model never actually wrong on the target and so makes negative transfer structurally impossible.

Shift vocabulary

Covariate shift P(x) changed but the rule P(y|x) did not. Everything slides together. In the generator this is α = 1.
Concept shift P(y|x) itself changed: classes have rearranged relative to each other, so the old boundary is genuinely in the wrong place. α = 0.
Negative transfer Adding correct new training data makes performance worse. Requires a boundary that is right for the source and wrong for the target.
EC number Enzyme Commission number, a four-level code for the reaction catalysed. This project uses level 3 (sub-subclass): level 4 encodes substrate specificity rather than chemistry, and roughly 83% of level-4 errors are correct through level 3.
Pfam family A homology group: proteins descended from a common ancestor with a shared domain architecture. Family and sequence similarity are nearly the same axis, which is why a family-conditioned measurement cannot separate "the embedding moved" from "the embedding stopped encoding function".
ESM-C 300M EvolutionaryScale protein language model, 960-dimensional mean-pooled embeddings. The best taxonomic classifier of any pLM tested, which is the largest interpretive risk in this project: we measure taxonomic transfer with the embedding most saturated in taxonomic signal.
ESM-2 650M Meta's protein language model, 1280-dimensional. Used for the model comparison on swissprot_esm2 and, from 13 August, on ec_esm2.
